ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
NPAs of State Finance Corporation 
*201. DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of State Finance Corporations are 
very sick and burdened with a large amount of Non-Performing Assets; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what manner Government proposes to rehabilitate the State Finance 
Corporations and deal with their large Non-Performing Assets? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH); (a) to (c) A Statement is placed on the Table -f the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Out of the 18 State Finance Corporations (SFCs) four, that is of, Delhi, 
Kerala, Rajasthan and West Bengal have a positive net worth as on 31 st March. 
2002. The net worth, however, of the remaining 14 SFCs stands fully eroded. 
The accumulated losses of all these SFCs, during 2001-02, aggregates to Rs. 
4,198 crores. NPAs of SFCs as a whole were 61% of the loans and advances, 
as at the end of Marcn 2002.1 he amount involved is Rs. 7076 crores. 
Standard Assets constitute only 39%. 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
(c) The SFCs Act was amended in 2000 for providing flexibility and 
functional autonomy to them. A Committee headed by Shri G.P. Gupta, the 
then CMD, IDBI looked into their functioning and submitted a report 
recommending, inter-alia, financial, operational and organisational re-
structuring of SFCs. The report of th e Committee has been sent to various 
SFCs for taking immediate action on recommendations that do not involve any 
financial support, such as operational a nd organisational restructuring. SFCs 
being State entities, the State Governme nts are the principal stakeholders. 
They are thus expected to consider steps for improving the performance and 
recapitalisation of SFCs. In order to attract long term refinance from Financial 
Institutions, SFCs have to improve recovery of NPAs and reestablish their 
viability.

Exploration of oil and natural gas in Krishna-Godawari basin 
*202. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of PETRO-
LEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present status of exploration of oil and natural gas in 
Krishna-Godawari basin in Andhra Pradesh by ONGC; 
(b) whether any headway has been achieved in finding oil and gas reserves 
in the basin; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS {SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Besides acquiring 32,574 Ground Line Kms. (GLK) of 2D and 
19,799 GLK of 3D of seismic data, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. 
(ONGC) has drilled 323 exploratory and 27 development wells in Krishna-
Godavari (KG) onland basin in the State of Andhra Pradesh as on 
01.10.2002.These exploratory efforts of ONGC in Andhra Pradesh have led to 
the discovery of 41 hydrocarbon finds, of which 8 are oil and gas finds and 33

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, my good friend and the hon. Member 
has drawn into the ambit of his question, a number of adventurous economic 
points, and I would endeavour to respond to each one of them. 
Firstly, I would say that his choice of the adjective that the interest rates 
have 'collapsed' is a disputable adj ective. We, of course, in the Finance 
Ministry, do not agree to the word 'colla pse'.This is a deliberate decision that 
has been taken progressively. The interest rate management is a function of 
the Central Bank, which is the Reserve Bank of India, and, certainly, in 
today's circumstances, for the hon. Member to suggest that there is any 
collapse of any kind in interest rates,  thereby suggesting that there is a 
deflationary situation, etc., when, in fact, manufacturing index Is going up, is 
very adventurous economic thinking. 
With regard to the second aspect of his question where he suggests that we 
have, in any sense, been persuaded by the interest rates management or the 
Reserve Bank of India has been persuaded by the management, in any form 
of competetion, with developed countries, I would say that no, we are not in 
competition with them. The Reserve Bank of India manages the interest rates 
entirely In accordance with the country's fiscal and monetary requirements. 
The third thing that he wishes to know is, will we be able to move back—
particularly, for the deposit interest rates—from say, roughly, 6 per cent to 13 
per cent? Frankly speaking. Madam, I do not see how, in the near future,-we 
can go back to a deposit rate system of 13 per cent. But, as I said just to a 
question earlier, that we, the Government, is fully alive to the difficulties that 
have been caused, in consequence, by a decline in the deposit rates, and we 
are addressing this question so that th e investor is somehow compensated for 
this.

Linking of Mahanadi with southern rivers 
*217. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Peninsular Grid linking Orissa's Mahanadi with major south 
ern rivers was found technically feasible in a study by National Water 
Development Agency; 
(b) whether this project if implemented, could go a long way in solving 
water scarcity problems of States of  Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra 
Pradesh; 
(c) whether this would save water of Mahanadi going waste and flowing 
into the sea; and 
(d) whether Government propose to take up this project, if so, by when? 
38 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES {SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI) : (a) to (d) tn 1980, the Ministry of Water Resources, then known as 
the Ministry of Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for 
integrated water resources development through inter-linkages of several 
southern-based Peninsular rivers and the Himalayan rivers. The Government 
of India established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) in 
1982 as an autonomous society to ca rryout water balance and feasibility 
studies of the Peninsular and Himalayan rivers. The -Peninsular Component 
of the National Perspective Plan envisages inter-llnking of Mahanadi-
Godavari-Krishna-Pennar-Cauvery-Vaigai. As per the water balance studies 
of various river basins of the penins ular Component conducted by National 
Water Development Agency, Mahanadi and Godavari river basins are surplus 
in water, whereas the river basins namely. Krishna, Pennar, Cauvery and 
Vaigai are deficit. It is. therefore, pr oposed to transfer the surplus water of 
Mahanadi which in turn will be receiving water from the Himalayan 
component and Godavari basins to Krishna basin by inter-linking Mahanadi 
to Godavari and Godavari to Krishna.  The water, thus received in Krishna 
basin is proposed to be transferred to Pennar, Cauvery and Vaigai basins. 
NWDA has identified 9 links under this part of the Peninsular Component for 
preparation of feasibility report and has prepared f easibility reports for three 
links. Implementation of the water transfer links would only be possible if the 
concerned co-basin States agree to the water linkage proposal and provide 
other logistical support necessary for project implementation and availability 
of fund is ensured.

companies, which came out with public  issues, have been identified as 
'vanishing companies'.

Commission of the State.

the States and suggest a plan by wh ich the Governments, collectively and 
severally, may bring about a restructuring of the public finances restoring

financing of Disaster Management wi th reference to the National Calam 
ity Contingency Fund and the Calami ty Relief Fund and make appropri

(RBI) contain several structural meas ures to improve the efficiency of 
financial system apart from monetary policy measures and signals for soft 
interest rate regime.

transparency in the conduct of monetary policy and provide information to

assessment of overall macro-economic situation. Initiatives of RBI towards a

Features of the Special VRS for the employees declared surplus 
(a) All permanent employees rendered surplus irrespective of their age and 
qualifying service can opt for the scheme. 
(b) An optee of Special VRS will be entitled to receive an ex-gratia 
amount equal to basic pay plus dearness allowance for the number of days 
worked out on the basis of length of service @ 35 days for each completed 
year and 25 days for each remaining year. For any part of a year, the number of 
days, for ex-gratia-amount, will be worked out on the basis of 365 days in a 
year. The ex-gratia amount will be further subject to the following conditions : 
(i)    Total number of years to be counted for payment of ex-gratia will 
not exceed 33 years; 
(ii)    No weightage of additional service will be given for the purpose 
of calculation of ex-gratia; 
(iii) The ex-gratia will be subject to a minimum of Rs. 25,000/- or 250 
days emoluments, whichever is higher; 
(iv) The ex-gratia amount should not exceed the sum of the basic pay 
plus DA that the employee would draw at the prevailing level for 
the balance of the period of service left before superannuation; 
(v)    The ex-gratia amount will be paid in lump sum; 
(vi) The ex-gratia amount up to Rs. 5.00 lakhs will be exempted from 
Income Tax;

given under CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972 to such permanent surplus 
employees who have rendered a minimum of 15 years of qualifying

Guidelines for foreign Banks 
1421. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are any guidelines i ssued by the Reserve Bank of India 
to regulate the functioning of foreign Banks in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the RBI exercises any effective control on these foreign Banks 
and if so, in what manner; 
(d) whether the foreign banks are permitted to close down their business in 
India at any time without due notice to concerned authorities; and 
(e) if so, the steps taken by the RBI in such cases to safeguard the 
96 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
deposits of the public? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is empowered under the Banking Regulation 
Act, 1949 to regulate functioning of all the banks in India, including foreign 
banks. All guidelines issued by RBI for regulating the functioning of banks in 
India are equally applicable to foreign banks. RBI's control over the foreign 
banks is the same as over domestic banks. 
(d) and (e) No, Sir.The foreign banks are required to give prior notice, to 
RBI, of their intention to close down their operations in India.The bank 
intending to close down its operation in India is required to discharge all its 
liabilities, realise assets and clear all obligations under contingent liabilities, 
before it is permitted by RBI to close operations in India. RBI ensures that 
foreign bank closes its operation in India only after meeting all liabilities in 
India including liabilities to depositors and investors.

Report on safe drinking water 
1504. SHRI CR THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of the report published by Third 
World Academy of Science on 'Safe Drinking Water'; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c)whether it is a fact that India has to face severe water scarcity as per the 
report; and 
(d) if so, the action proposed by Government to deal with the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The report published by Third World Academy of Science on "Safe 
Drinking Water" states that the majority of the world's population does not 
have access to safe drinking water. This is certainly true in most parts of 
Africa and Asia. Even in relatively adva nced countries such as India, safe 
drinking water is not readily available, particularly in rural areas. Together 
these sources account for just 1 per cen t of all water on earth. Six billion 
people depend on freshwater supply (available from rivers, lakes, 
underground sources and aquifers) and a significant portion of the world's 
population now face water shortages. Today 31 countries representing 2.8 
billion people, including China, India, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Peru, 
confront chronic water problems. Total withdrawals of freshwater have 
increased dramatically in 
165 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2002] 
recent times. The groundwater aquifers are currently being depleted faster 
than they are being replenished in parts of India, China and the United States. 
The report narrates some success stories of augmenting supply of water and 
water harvesting and community farming in Rajasthan achieved by Tarun 
Bharat Sangh. The report also speaks about ways to save and replenish water, 
making water safe and potable, making waste water fit for use again and 
technology to make safe drinking water. 
(c) The average annual water availability in the river-systems of the 
country is assessed at 1869 Billion C ubic Metre (BCM). According to the 
International Criteria, a situation of annual water availability of less than 1000 
cubic metre per capita is considered as scarcity condition. The per capita 
water availability in India is 1820 cubic metre per year (2001). However, due 
to spatial variability of rain in the co untry and also because of variation in 
population density, per capita average annual availability of water in different 
basins presently varies from 16,990 cubic metre in Minor River Basins draining 
into Bangladesh & Myanmar, 13,636 cubic metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin 
to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. Presently, per capita water availability 
in some river basins namely. Area of  Inland Drainage in Rajasthan Desert; 
Sabarmati; East Flowing Rivers between Mahanadi and Kanyakumari; Pennar; 
West Flowing Rivers of Kutchh, Saurashtra including Luni; Cauvery; Tapi and 
Mahi is in scarcity cdondition. Further, temporal variability in rainfall also 
creates temporary scarcity of water in certain years. In year 2025, the per 
capita water availability has been estimated as 1341 cubic metre per year on a 
national level. The river basins Krishna, Subarnarekha and Ganga are also 
likely to come under the category ot scarce basins. 
(d) To address the problem of water scarcity in the country, emphasis is 
being made to augmei*:t storages through constructioa of dams, speedy 
completion of ongoing water resources projects, other means for water 
harvesting and conservation, and non-conventionaJ measures like interlinking 
of rivers. The National Perspective Plan for water resources development 
envisages interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers 
for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins to provide 
benefits of drinking water supply, irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, 
navigation, fisheries, salinity and pollution control etc.

Distress sale of Paddy by farmers In Andhra Pradesh 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairman, this year, my home State, Andhra Pradesh, has experienced the 
w/orst drought. As reported, the rainfall was 34 per cent less than the normal 
rainfall. Despite this, the paddy grower s have grown their crop in whatever 
way they can. Normally, 7 million tonnes of paddy is grown in the State, but 
it is estimated that this year, the paddy yield is around 48 lakh tonnes only, 
which has affected the farmers very ba dly. But the miseries of the hapless 
farmers are far from over, as the paddy is lying unsold with them. There are 
no takers for the paddy in the State. The Food Corporation of India is not 
purchasing the paddy under one pretext or the other. The rice mill owners too 
are reluctant to purchase the paddy, l eaving the farmers high and dry. Thus, 
practically, the MSP declared for paddy has become redundan t in the State. 
The paddy farmers have started distress sale of their produce, resulting in a 
great loss to the farmers of the State. 
1, therefore, earnestly appeal to the Central Government to come to 
the rescue of the poor paddy growers of Andhra Pradesh and direct the FCI 
and other Government agencies to purchase the entire paddy stock of the 
farmers at the MSP declared by the Go vernment, without further loss of time, 
and save the paddy farmers of Andhra Pradesh who might resort to 
194 

[3 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the extreme step of committing suicide, if the situation is not checked in time.   
Thank you. Sir. 
Demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to Central University 
MS. PRAMII-A BOHIDAR (Orissa):  Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
the Sambalpur University serves as the chief educational centre for the entire 
western parts of Orissa. The Sambalpur University was established on is'" 
January, 1967. It is  the second biggest affiliating University in the State of 
Orissa, with jurisdiction exceeding over ten districts of the western parts of 
Orissa. They are Sambalpur, Sundergarh, Bargarh, Jharsuguda, Bolangir, 
Deogarh, Soudh, Suvernapur, Kalahandi, Nuapara and Athamallik subdivision 
of Angul. 
The entire area under the jurisdicti on of this University in Western 
Onssa is both economically and educa tionally backward. The Government of 
India has launched the KBK Programme  in these districts to eradicate 
backwardness. The Scheduled Castes an d the Scheduled Tribes constitute 46 
per cent of the total population of this region, against the Orissa State average 
of 38 per cent and the nati onal average of 22 per cent. The Scheduled Castes, 
the Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes constitute more than 90 
per cent of the total population in this region. Out of a total of 87 very 
backward blocks in Orissa, 67 blocks are located in Western Orissa. 
In the absence of adequate fund, the State Government, in spite of 
its eagerness and willingness to help the University, is unable to do so. 
Unless the Central Government comes to its aid, this University, created to 
serve a backward region of the country,' is sure to suffer stagnation and 
become irrelevant to the socio-economic grovirth of the region. 
Orissa does not have any Central University, at present. In view of 
the above-mentioned facts, the Central Government should consider our 
demand for upgrading Sambalpur University to a Central University. Thank 
you.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Na du): Sir. the Unit Trust of 
India is a statutory corporation, established under the Unit Trust of India Act,

High dividends, sale and repurchase price of units, unrelated to the 
actual earnings, and other shortcomings in the UTI's working led to a fall in 
the Net Asset Value of the units. These inherent weaknesses, coupled with the 
problems of the capital market in March, 2001, resulted In the US-64 Scheme 
facing a substantial redemption during the months of April-May, 2001, 
forcing temporary suspension of the sale and repurchase under the US-64 
Schemefor a period of six months, that is. up to   31^' December, 2001. 
Depressed capital market and the serious move to restrict the 
Government's liability resulted in the bifurcation of the UTI into two parts, 
namely, Unit-I, comprising the guaranteed portion, and Unit-ll, comprising all 
Net Asset Value-based Schemes, and. in the repeal of the UTI Act, 1963. This 
division provides for and facilitates bifurcation of assets and liabilities of the 
UTI into two parts, that is, specified undertakings and specified companies, 
thereby distancing the Central Government from the UTI and Mutual Fund 
activities.

Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir.

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, IN CHARGE OF THE MINISTRY OF 
HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Madam, the hon. Member is right that 
we do not have any Extradition Treaty w ith Portugal. Therefore, immediately 
after it was informed on 19th September that Abu Salem has been arrested in 
Lisbon, — he was on our wanted list — the Minister of External Affairs wrote a 
formal letter to the Portugal Government requesting that he be extradited to India, 
because a number of cases relating to serious offences are pending against him 
in Indian courts. Subsequently, the CBI team went there.The Embassy in Lisbon 
provided full assistance to our team.The CBI team had had elaborate discussions 
with Portuguese authorities.The Portuguese authorities were, all along, helpful. At 
no point of time, did we come across any difficulty, but they said that we have 
to proceed as per law. And, as per law, a formal extradition request has to come 
from the Government of India on the cases pending against him, with the 
requisite FIRs, evidences, etc.These are required to be furnished. Furthermore, 
under the Portuguese law, there is not provision of capital punishment. And, 
they do not extradite a person who can be given capital punishment in another 
country. So, they would like to have an assurance from the Government of India 
that even after being extradited, he would not be subjected to capital 
punishment. It will require the State Governments to give all the necessary 
evidence and get it translated in Portuguese. All this process takes its own 
time. They have assured us that, at the moment, he is being tried or he is being 
investigated in relation to offences committed there in Portugal under the 
violation of the law of immigration and so many other laws. They have said 
that 'you may rest assured that we are not going to release him, and, in the 
meanwhile, you complete your process.' They have taken a remand of 90 days. So, 
within those 90 days, the process required from the Government of India would 
be completed. And, we are hopeful that Abu Salem would be extradited to India.

Terrorist activities from Bhutan 
*222.  SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the militants are 
carrying on terrorist activities on a large scale from Bhutan alongwith the 
Assam-Bhutan border; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken/proposed to be taken in 
this regard? 
(c) whether the Central Government have received any request from the 
State Government of Assam to flush out National Democratic Font for Bodoland 
(N.D.F.B.) militants; if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto and steps contemplated in this 
direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY FOR HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI) :(a) to (d) The Government is aware about the existence of 
camps of Indian insurgent groups including National Democratic Front of 
Bodoland (NDFB) in Bhutan territory, which are being used by them for safe 
havens, sanctuary, training purposes and launching of operations against 
Indian civilians and security forces. The Government of Assam have also 
drawn the attention of the Central Government in this regard. 
The matter regarding removal of camps of Indian insurgent groups from 
Bhutan territory has been taken up from time to time with the Royal 
Government of Bhutan (RGOB). The issue was also discussed in detail during 
the visits of External Affairs Minister of Bhutan from August 4 to 6, 2002 and 
Foreign Secretary from October 28 to 30, 2002, with the Bhutanese 
leadership. The RGOB have assured that they will not allow these elements to 
use their territory for activities prejudicial to the interests of India.

Madhya Pradesh 
1602. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) how many villages in Madhya Pradesh have been electrified with the 
help of solar energy cells during the last three years; 
(b) what is the potential of electricity connection using solar energy in the 
State; 
(c) the steps taken by Government to exploit the potential in the State; 
and 
(d) how much of funds have been allotted to Madhya Pradesh under the 
Solar Village Electrification Scheme during this year? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) The 
Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources initiated a programme during 2001 -
02 for the electrification of villages in remote and difficult areas in the entire 
country including the State of Madhya Pradesh, through installation of suitable 
systems based on locally available renewable energy sources, like solar 
photovoltaic (SPV) systems & power plants, small hydro units and biomass 
gasifier systems. 
116 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
The Madhya Pradesh Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (PMUVN), Bhopal, is the 
nodal agency for implementation of solar energy based village electrification 
programme in the State. The MPUVN has distributed solar lanterns and installed 
a solar powered TV set in one village in the State i.e. village Mathar of Block 
and Tehsil Budhni in District Sehore during the last three years. 
The MPUVN has, however, identified 1,225 villages in the remote and 
far flung areas in the State for elect rification through renewable energy 
technologies/options, it is estimated that 80% of these villages could be 
electrified through SPV systems and power plants.The Ministry is, however, yet to 
receive Specific Project Proposals from MPUVN for sanction. 
Earlier a proposal was developed by the Ministry for electrification of 9 
tribal villages in the Jabalpur Parliamentary Constituency at a total estimated 
cost of about Rs. 91 lakhs, but the project could not be sanctioned as the 
balance funds required for implementation of the project, after taking into account 
the admissible support from the Ministry, Could not be provided by the State 
Government or under the MPLAD Scheme. 
No funds have been released to the MPUVN so far during the current year for 
electrification of remote villages through solar energy.

†1605. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Dabhol Power Project was started with the loans 
and advanced by the financial institutions of the country; 
(b) if so, the total amount spent so far by these institutions on the maintenance and 
running, along with the cost of construction of the project; and 
(c) the percentage of the said amount of the total expenditure made thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) The Dabhol Power Project was constructed using a mix of 
equity and loan funds.The equity was brought in by the sponsors viz. Enron, General 
Electric, Bechtel and the Maharashtra Power Development Corporation Limited 
(MPDCL).The loan 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
funds were advanced by a consortium of off-shore banks and Indian Financial

(b) and (c) The exposure of the IFIs as on date aggregates Rs. 6551 crores 
(Rs. 3292 crores by way of fund based assistance and Rs. 3259 crores by way 
of guarantes). Phase-I of the project had commenced commercial operations 
in May, 1999, while Phase-ll was under construction. Phase-ll of the project 
was complete to the extent of around 92% as on 31 -5-2001. Due to certain

Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB), MSEB stopped taking power

2001 onwards, the expenditure on asset preservation, security and payment of 
insurance premia, was being incurred out of funds available in the accounts of 
DPC. From September, 2002 onwards, after depletion of funds in the accounts of 
DPC, the principal IFIs have been incurring this expenditure. As on December 
2,2002, IFIs have incurred an expend iture of Rs. 7.26 crores for asset 
preservation, security and insurance premia.

1607.   SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Indraprastha Power Generation

Modernization (R&M) work in all the four units of Indraprastha Power Plant (3 x 
62.5 MW +1 x 60 MW). The job of comprehensive study of R&M for the 
station has been entrusted to National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC).

IPGCL. At present the station is operating at an average PLF of about 40% for 
the last 4 years. The maximum available out put of all the four units is ranging 
from 45 MW to 50 MW. After R&M, the station will operate at the installed 
name plate capacity of 247.5 MW with life extension of 10-15 years. The work 
is expected to be completed within 5 years.

Statement 
Details of the Power Sector Reform Fund 
As a part of measures to refo rm the power sector, the Committee 
recommended that State Government should consolidate the past liabilities and 
finance them through agreements for write-downs and future sector surpluses. 
However, going by the track record of State Governments, a mere statement of 
intent is unlikely to carry any weight from the other stakeholders, specifically 
existing creditors and prospective lenders. In order to enhance the credibility and 
mitigate the risk of policy reversals it is necessary to ring-fence both the 
liabilities and the inflows earmarked for the sector restructuring. In order to do 
this, the State Government should establish a Power Sector Reform Fund 
(PSRF). All existing liabilities of the sector should be transferred to the PSRF. 
The responsibility for servicing these liabilities, however, remains with the 
State Government and as noted later, these can be re-financed on better terms 
with Central Government support. Conc omitantly, existing receivables (the 
privatized utility can be contracted to recover them the on an incentive-sharing 
basis), privatisation proceeds, and gran ts from the Government of India and 
other donor agencies should be transferred to the PSRF to defray these 
liabilities. In addition, it wo uld receive a portion of the surplus from future 
operations as revenues, say, in the form of a PSRF surcharge, The PSRF 
would be drawn Upon in a pre-specified order of priority to meet the State 
Government's obligations in discharging its liabilities.

Rejection of Delhi Declaration at the climate change meet 
by the EU 
1618. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that European Union has rejected the draft of the 
Delhi Declaration circulated by the Indian Government at the climate change 
meet; 
(b) if so, what are the details of the draft circulated; and 
(c) what are the reasons given by the European Union for rejecting it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The European Union did not 
reject the draft of the Delhi Declaration. A group of developed countries, 
including the European Union wanted to initiate a process for beginning a 
dialogue on broader participation of countries in greenhouse gas mitigation 
commitments for period beyond 2012. This  was resisted successfully by the 
developing countries, including India, on the grounds that the per capita 
greenhouse gas emissions of the developing countries, in general, were low in 
comparison to the developed countries, and that the overriding priority for the 
developing countries was poverty eradication for which economic growth was 
essential. The Delhi Ministerial Declaration on Climate Change and Sustainable 
Development was adopted by all Parties as a consensus document.

last five years, State-wise, is enclosed [See Appendix 197 Annexure No. 14].

Supply during the last five years is enclosed. [See Appendix 197 Annexure No.

The following noms and criteria are being adopted under Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme for providing drinking water to rural population in 
the habitations: 
(a) 40 liters per capita per day (Ipcd) of safe drinking water for human 
beings. 
(b) 30 Ipcd additional for cattle in the Desert Development Programme 
Areas. 
(c) One hand-pump or stand post for every 250 persons. 
(d) The water source should exist within the habitation/within 1.6 km in the 
plains and within 100 mtrs. elevation in the hilly areas. 
[Water is defined as safe if it is free from biological contamination 
(guinea worms, cholera, typhoid etc.) and chemical contamination (excess fluoride, 
brackishness, iron, arsenic, nitrates)] 
Recently Government of India have approved the relaxations in the rural 
water supply norms in the following manner: - 
(a) The norms may be relaxed to provide for 55 Itrs. per capita per day 
with a source within 0.5 km in the plains and 50 metres elevation in 
the hills after the coverage of a ll Not Covered and Partially Covered 
rural habitations in that State is achieved, as per the existing norms of 
40 litres per capita per day. This relaxation is subject to the condition that 
beneficiaries of the relaxed norms will share a part of the capital cost 
(which should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities 
for subsequent Operation and Maintenance. 
(b) In case of schemes in quality affe cted villages or in multi-village 
schemes where the capital cost is very high, the schemes could be 
executed and implemented by the Government Departments/ 
Agencies/Board, and water is supplied to individual villages at 
157

village, the beneficiaries would share a part of the capital cost (which 
should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities for 
subsequent Operation and Maintenance of the village water distrbution 
network, while Government Department/ Board/Agency would maintian 
the main water supply system upto the village. 
Governments/Board/Agency may also charge water rates to the 
Panchayats/Village communities for bulk supply of water for drinking 
purpose. Such water charges and the village Operation and 
Maintenance cost would be fully met by the users/ beneficiaries. 
As per recent information available out of 50,379 rural habitations in

nowhere near the targeted figures, which were projected at the initial stage of 
the Budget. We are not going to discu ss the Tenth Five-Year Plan, as it has 
not yet been approved by the N.D.C. But, what we find that Rs.78,000 crores 
will be realised through the route of disinvestment. The contemporary events, 
and also the sharp differences in the Council of Ministers on the issue of 
disinvestment,' as reported in the news papers, we find that apart from the 
concept of joint responsibility, sacrificing in a parliamentary form of 
Government. It raises substantial issues is not desirable that Ministers should 
express their views, air their individual opinions, publicly.   But, those were 
the traditions of the past.   We are living

Statement 
The employment exchanges are under the administrative and financial control 
of the respective States/UT Governments and these are being modernized 
according to their financial capacity. At  present 363 out of 939 employment 
exchanges are computerized. 
Reliable estimates of employment and unemployment are obtained from the 
quinquennial labour force surveys conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organisation. Job-seekers registered with the employment exchanges are not 
necessarily unemployed and it is also not necessary that all the unemployed 
should register with the employment exchanges. Therefore, the employment 
exchange data provides details of the job seekers registered and not the 
complete picture of unemployment in the country. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, my question focuses on the statistical data 
about unemployment which is primarily obtained from the employment exchanges 
in the organised sector. Of course, in the unorganised sector, only sample surveys 
are done. So, the quality of data is hardly useful. As you know, Sir, in the 
Western countries the rate of unemploym ent is a very crucial parameter for 
the evaluation of the economy. We have no such reliable data about the exact 
number of unemployed people. The employment exchanges work at more than 
900 places and they collect data only from establishments which are employing 
more than 25 people in the organised sector. There is the Compulsory Notification 
of Vacancies Act. But the employment exchanges are monitored by the State 
Governments. What is the punitive action taken against the companies which 
do not notify vacancies? Our experience is that nobody bothers to inform the 
employment exchanges about the exis ting vacancies. They advertise the 
vacancies in the newspapers. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You have already put your question. Let him answer. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: I would like to know whether the 
Compulsory Notification of Vacancies Act is being followed or not.

Supply of rice to BPL families 
*244. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news report captioned "Right 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
to food still a dream" which appeared in The Hindu' dated the 24th October, 2002; 
(b) if so, what steps would be taken to provide rice to families Living Below 
the Poverty Line as directed by the Supreme Court; 
(c) what action Government propose to take so that price of the rice through 
ration shop is fixed as per the purchasing capacity of these families living in 
extreme poverty; 
(d) whether any action plan is proposed to be formulated to help villagers 
in various parts of the country who are bracing themselves for extreme hunger 
in months ahead due to crop failure; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND- PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) The Central Government have been making allocations of 
foodgrains under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) to the State 
Governments and UT Administrations for distribution amongst the BPL 
families @ 35 kg per family per month. The Central Issue Prices for the BPL 
families are highly subsidized and have remained unchanged since July, 2000. 
In order to address the needs of one crore poorest of the poor families, the 
Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) is being implemented in all parts of the country 
under which foodgrains are issued @ Rs. 2 a kg for wheat and Rs. 3 a kg for 
rice at the retail level.Under the Special Component of the Sampoorna Gramin 
Rojgar Yojana (SGRY), the foodgrains are provided, free of cost, to the States 
affected by natural calamities such as flood, cyclone and drought for 
generation of additional employment oppo rtunities, alongwith food security, 
through creation of durable community assets in the rural areas. So, far, about 
38.29 lakh MTs of foodgrains have been allotted to 16 drought/natural calamity 
affected States under the Special Component of the SGRY during the current 
financial year.

Number of BPL people 
†260. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Planning Commission has taken a decision to ascertain the 
number of people living Below Poverty Line in each State; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, whether Government had also finalized any policy to ascertain such 
numbers; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the difference between the old and new 
procedure and policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) The Planning Commission 
has been estimating the incidence of pov erty at National and State level since 
the late 1970s. The estimates of poverty were initially made from the method 
outlined in the Task Force on Projection of Minimum Needs and Effective 
Consumption Demand. Th is method was replaced by the methodology 
contained in the Report of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion and 
Number of Poor {commonly known as Lakdawala Committee, named after its 
Chairman) in March 1997 to estimate the poverty ratio (also known as the 
Head-Count ratio) at National and State level. According to this method, the 
percentage of people below the poverty line is estimated from state-specific 
poverty lines and state-specific consumer expenditure distribution, obtained from 
the large sample surveys on household consumer expenditure conducted by the 
NSSO once in approximately five years. Using this method, the poverty 
estimates of all the previous years have been re-worked and are available for 
the years 1973-74, 1977-78,1983,1987-88, 1993-94 and 1999-2000. 
(c) The Planning Commission in 1977 constituted a Task Force on 
Minimum Needs and Effective Consumption Demands which defined the 
poverty line as per capita expenditure level at which the average per capita per 
day calorie in take was 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas.The 
monetary equivalent of these norms were calculated as monthly per capita 
consumption expenditure of Rs.49.09 in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 in urban areas 
for 1973-74.These poverty lines were applied uniformly to all the States. Second, 
in order to ensure consistency with the national aggregates, the NSS consumer 
expenditure data was adjusted to the level of CSO consumption on a pro-rata basis 
across all expenditure classes. Using the poverty lines and the adjusted 
expenditure class-wise distribution of persons obtained from the national sample 
survey data on consumer expenditure of the States, the State-wise estimates of 
poverty were made. 
This methodology for estimation of poverty at National and State level 
was regarded by some as inappropriate and even inadequate in 
38 

[5 December. 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
giving a representative picture of incidence of poverty in India. In September 
1989, Planning Commission constituted an Expert Group to look into the 
methodology for estimation of poverty and to redefine the poverty line, if 
necessary. The Expert Group submitted its Report in July, 1993. 
The Expert Group did no t redefine the poverty line and accepted the one 
defined by the Task Force which was at national level. However, it 
recommended the disaggregation of the national poverty line into state-wise 
poverty lines in order to reflect the State-wise price differential. The important 
points of departure between the Expert Group methodology and the Task 
Force methodology are: 
(a) tn the new method, the NSS consumption expenditure data are not 
adjusted in any way and it is used as It is. 
(b) The new method uses State-wise poverty lines as against national level 
poverty line used in the old method. 
(c) The new method uses State-specific cost of Irving indices for updating the 
poverty line separately in rural and urban areas.The old method used only one 
all-India Index which is also same for rural and urban areas. 
The full Planning Commission under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister 
accepted its recommendations with minor modifications in March, 1997.

Quality of Telecom Service 
1668. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHONOLGY be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the overall level of quality of 
service in the Indian Telecom Sector has been found to be poor despite 
registering impressive growth in the past few years; 
(b) if so, whether the TRAI has found in its first survey on quality 
standards that private operators were  providing comparatively better quality 
of service than BSNL and MTNL; 
(c) if so, the details of the said survey report; and 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December. 2002] 
(d) the action taken by Government to improve the quality of service In the 
Indian Telecom Sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SANJAY PASWAN): (a) Sir, the survey  conducted by TRAI through M/s. 
Indian Market Research Bureau (IMRB) during October-December 2001, has 
revealed that most of the Tetecom se rvice providers were not meeting the 
prescribed benchmarks on quality of service. 
(b) In its first quarterly survey report on quality standards, TRAI has 
found that none of the basic operators were meeting the quality of service 
(QOS) norms stipulated in the QOS regu lations of TRAI. As per the survey, 
the private operators who operate in va stly different scale of operation and 
have hardly any significant presence in the rural areas where the problems of 
maintenance are more complex, have been able to provide comparatively 
better quality of services than MTNL & BSNL. Also, while MTNL & BSNL 
have the legacy equipment, the private operators have latest technology 
equipment and gadgets. Noticeably, TRAI survey has also found that the five 
best performers in the area of basic serv ices on the basis of weighted average 
score for various customers satisfaction parameters, are the MTNL, Mumbai 
and four circles of BSNL viz. Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and 
Andhra Pradesh. 
(c) As part of the TRAI's mandate to conduct periodical surveys for 
determining quality of Telecom services in the country, the Authority had 
selected M/s. Indian Market Resear ch Bureau (IMRB), a well established 
research organisation to perform the following two functions: 
 
> objective assessment of quality for service provided by both basic 
as well as cellular service providers  with reference to the Quality 
of service (QOS) standards prescribed by the TRAI. 
> Subjective survey of the level of consumer satisfaction with the 
services. 
The first quarterly survey was carried out during the period from October 
to December 2001. A sample size of 317 exchanges of basic service operators 
and all cellular service operators were covered in the survey. The overall 
performance of the basic service operators were 
64 

[5 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
assesed on the basis of some select parameters such as customer complaints 
on phone faults, percentage of new connections given in fifteen days, shifting 
completed within five days, closures in 24 hours, level of operator service 
response, average time taken to attend customer complaints, percantage of bills 
disputed by customers etc. In the case of cellular services, besides fault and 
billing complaints percentage of calls dropped during conversation, 
percentage of calls with good quality of voice were some of the parameters 
measured. 
The consumers surveyed generally felt that the overall quality of service 
needs to be improved. Level of satisfaction regarding service provision, 
network performance and help services were found to be very low. The 
survey findings also suggest that none of the basic operators including the 
incumbents, are meeting the QOS norms stipulated in the QOS regulations. 
(d) Actions being taken by BSNL & MTNL to improve quality of 
Telecom. Services. Improvement in the quality of service is a continuous 
process. Following steps are being taken by BSNL & fvlTNL to improve the 
basic services : 
(i)     Replacement of underground paper core cables by Jelly filled 
cables. 
(ii)      Lying of cables in ducts. 
(iii) Laying of underground cables right up to the subscribes premises so 
as to eliminate drop wires. Introduction of 5 pair undergorund 
cable is one such move in this regard. 
(iv) Opening of more and more remote line units thereby reducing area to 
be served by each exchange with a corresponding reduction in the 
size of the outdoor plant. 
(v)     Replacement of old telephone instruments. 
{vij Introduction ot new technology e.g. Wireless in Local Loop, DLC, 
etc. to eliminate the need for underground cables. 
(vii) Periodic dressing of external plant. 
(viii) Pagers to line staff/field staff wherever feasible. 
(ix) Mopttonng of faults by senior officers. 
(x) Arrangement for fault booking on 198 centrally at Short 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
Distance Charging Centre (SDCC) on Interactive Voice Response 
Systenr) (IVRS). 
(xi) Computerisation of Fault Repair Service (FRS) at more & more 
places. 
In addition, MTNL is taking following steps to improve quality of Cellular 
Mobile Services : 
(i)     A dedicated network management group has been deployed. 
(ii) Continuous monitoring through drive tests is being carried out and 
RF optimisation is done to improve RF signal strength. 
-(ili)     The software bugs in billing system have been removed and 
regular bills are being issued. 
(iv) To improve customer interface, a full fledged call centre with IVRS 
facility is being set up. In addition to existing three Customer Care 
Centres, another five Customer Care Centres are being opened. 
(v) To facilitate the bill payment, billing counters have been opened in 
different localities. In addition, bill viewing and payment through 
Internet and cheque collections through drop boxes provided by 
Banks have also been arranged.

Teledensity through WLL Technology 
1673. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY : Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state : 
(a) whether It is a fact that there is possibility to increase teledensity 
through WLL technology at comparatively lesser cost than the fixed 
telephone lines; 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof with elucidation in comparative terms the salient 
features of the fixed line telephone and WLL-technology based telephone; 
(c) the steps taken by Government to increase the tele-density adopting 
WLL technology within the next two financial year; 
 
(d) whether Government are considering to achieve the target through 
reduced rent and tariff on WLL based telephones; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SANJAY PASWAN) : (a) and (b) WLL (Wireless in Local Loop) is playing an 
Important role in deployment of telephones in the country. However, it is not 
possible to establish a definite correlation between tele-density and the cost of 
provision of WLL as tele-density depends upon provision of telephones which 
in turn depends upon demands for telephones. The salient features of fixed 
lines telephones and WLL technology based telephones are : 
In fixed line telephones, connections are provided through a pair of 
normally copper cable to each subs criber, whereas in WLL system 
connections are provided on wireless technology Laying of underground cable is 
time consuming, whereas WLL deployment is fast. Interruption in service will 
be there whenever cable is cut in fixed line connections due to man 
made/natural calamities, whereas interruption in WLL are not dependent on 
such eventualities except equipment fault. Fixed line telephone on copper cable 
are able to provide higher data rates compared to the presently deployed WLL 
systems though in future deployments this difference will disappear. 
(c) The Government through its Public sector units i.e. Bharat Sanchar 
Nigam Limited (BSNL) & Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL) 
are planning to deploy 29^7 lakh lines on WLL during the next two 
financial years. 
(d) and (e) Tariff is fixed by Telecom Regulatory Authority of India 
(TRAI) who have absolute powers to fix it and Government has no rote 
in tariff fixation.

1696. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the quantum of dues the sugar mills in the country owe to 
the sugarcane growers, State-wise; and 
(b) the steps taken to ensure clearance of dues by the sugar mills in a time 
bound programme to avert unhappy situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) A statement showing State-wise position of sugarcane price 
payable, price paid and the balance outstanding for the season 2001 -2002, as 
on 30.9.2002 is annexed. {See below) 
(b) The responsibility for ensuring timely payment of cane price dues lies 
with the State Governments which have necessary powers and field 
organizations to enforce such payments. The Central Government on its part, 
besides writing to the State Governments from time to time for expeditious 
clearance of the same, has taken the fo llowing remedial measures to improve 
the financial health of domestic sugar industry with a view to enabling it to 
reduce the cane price arrears: 
(i) The levy obligation of domestic sugar factories was reduced from 40% 
to 30% with effect from 01.01.2000 and, subsequently, to 15% with 
effect from 01.02.2001; this has further been reduced to 10% with effect 
from 01.03.2002 and will enable the sugar factories to sell more 
sugar under free sale quota In the open market and obtain better 
realization. 
(ii) To restrict the inflow of imported sugar in the country, the Central 
Government (with effect from 09.02.2000) has increased the 
customs duty to 60% along with the existing countervailing duty of 
Rs. 850 per tonne. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [5 December, 2002] 
(iii) The Central Government is pursuing a policy of encouraging stability and 
reasonable level of sugar prices in the domestic market through judicious 
releases of free sale sugar quotas to enable the sugar factories to clear 
the cane price dues of the farmers. 
(iv) In order to liquidate the stocks of the sugar mills, the Government has 
allowed export of sugar. The quantitative ceiling on export of sugar as 
well as the requirement of registration with Agricultural and 
Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) 
have been dispensed with, with effect from 01.04.2001. 
(v) In order to encourage the export of sugar, the Sugar Development Fund 
(SDF) Act, 1982 and the SDF Rules, 1983 have been amended, 
enabling reimbursement of the inte rnal transport & freight charges 
on export shipments of sugar. 
(vi) The Government has decided to create a buffer stock of 20 lakh tonnes 
of sugar for a period of one year. This will enable the sugar mills to 
get a subsidy amount of Rs. 412 crore from the Sugar Development 
Fund. In addition, an amount of Rs. 374 crores would be available 
from the banks to the mills on account  of buffer stock. Thus, a total 
amount of Rs. 786 crores would be provided to the mills enabling 
them to clear the payment of cane price dues to the sugarcane growers. 
This will also help the sugar industry to mitigate the financial 
hardship.

† 1777. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY : Will the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the latest status of construction of National Highway 57; 
(b) the amount sanctioned by Government for highway during 2001-2002 
and 2002-2003 and the works on which the same was spent; 
(c) whether many parts of the highway are in a very bad condition and 
need to be strengthened urgently; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the action Government are taking in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD TRANS-
PORT AND HIGHWAYS [MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI]: (a) and 
(b) On National Highway 57, two estimates for improvement of riding quality 
works in a length of 16 km, three estimates for periodical renewal works in a 
length of 52.43 km and six estimates for construction of bridges, amounting to 
Rs. 258.57 lakh, Rs. 442.99 lakh and Rs. 433.97 lakh respectively were 
sanctioned by the Ministry during 2001-02. This National Highway also 
forms part of East-West Corridor of National Highways Development Project 
(NHDP) being implemented by the National Highway Authority of India 
(NHAI). The maintenance of the National Highway is still being continued 
with the State Road Construction Department by NHAI, until four-laning 
work is taken up. An amount of Rs. 61.40 lakh during 2002-03 has been 
released to the State Road Construction Department by NHAI, on an ad-hoc 
basis, for repair and maintenance. 
(c) and (d) Out of 310 kms length of NH-57, there is a missing link, 
approximately 50 km length including bridge across river Kosi. Construction of 
this missing link and strengthening in the remaining stretches would be taken up 
along with the four laning of National Highway 57. Model studies for fixation 
of site and alignment of Kosi bridge is already in progress and is targeted to be 
completed by February 2003. Project preparation of four laning of this National 
Highway, including strengthening, is proposed to be taken up in 2003-04 by 
NHAI and construction is targeted to be taken up In 2004-05. The entire 
project is targeted to be completed by December 2007.

SSIs Role in Economy 
1780. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the role played by the small scale Industries in the 
economy today; 
(b) how it differs from the role played in seventies and eighties; 
(c) whether its role has diminished due to liberalisation of the  economy; 
and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) The small 
scale industries have been playing a significant role in the Indian economy in terms 
of industrial productton, employment generation and exportsThe role of the SSI 
sector has not changed since the seventies and eighties. At present, the SSI sector 
contributes 39% of industrial production, 34% in national exports and provided 
employment to over 192 lalth persons in 2001-02. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. In fact, the sector has emerged as a vibrant constituent ot the 
economy and is well equipped to face the challenge of liberalisation. A 
Comprehensive Policy Pacitage announced in August, 2000 contains several 
measures to further strengthen this sector both domestically and globally. The 
SSI sector has been assigned an important role in employment generation during 
the Tenth Five Year Plan. In the context of the announcement made by the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister for generating 50 million additional jobs in the country 
during this period, the SSI sector has t)een assigned the task of creating 4.4 
million additional jobs.

Threat posed to Dolphins in Chilka Lake 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Madam, tourist boats in 
Chilka lake of Orissa are causing a se rious threat to the life of dolphins. 
According to the Wildlife Society of Orissa, 11 dolphins were killed during the 
last two years. Two dolphins were killed last month. Recognised as an 
endangered specie, the Irrawady dolphins (Orcealla Brevirostris). numbering 
55 are a unique natural heritage of Orissa, Chilka lake is one of the only two 
places in the world where these mammals are seen, the other being Songkhia 
lake in Thailand. 
Propellers of tourist boats kill or  seriously injure these dolphins 
whenever boats surround them. Curious t ourists always want to have a closer 
look at this rare mammal. With t he promotion of tour ism by the State 
Government, there has been a quantum jump in the number of tourists visiting 
Chilka, especially in winter. But, the tourism sans necessary precautions. It is 
becoming an encroachment on the rights of these animals. 
In view of their endangered status, these dolphins should receive the 
highest level of protection under law. It is true that tourism earns revenue for 
the country. But, at the same time, preserving our natural wealth and heritage 
should not be compromised with money, The Government should go in for 
projects like eco-tourism, which has been successfully experimented in Kerala.

Enhancement of royalty on lignite at par with group-Vcoal 
SHR! R. KAMARAJ fTarnil Nadu): Madam Deputy Chairman, my 
Special Mention is about tlie royalty on Neyveli lignite. The Government of 
India, in the Ministry of Energy, Department of Coal, decided in August, 1990, 
to pay royalty on lignite, by treating it  on par with Group V Coal. Therefore, the 
royalty for group V coal as well as lignite was fixed at Rs.2.50 per tonne. 
However, when the Government of Indi a raised the royalty on Group V coal to 
Rs. 25 per tonne in 1991, and to Rs. 50 per tonne in 1994, the royalty on lignite 
remained at Rs. 2.50 per tonne. The Tamil Nadu Government had repeatedly 
urged the Government of India to trea t the State on par wit h the other States 
that are benefited from the periodic revisi on of royalty, and made it clear that 
Tamil Nadu felt discriminated against by the retention of the old royalty rate, 
when the royalty on coal of equal parity had been increased twice. Finally, in 
March, 2001, the Ministry of Coal increas ed the royalty on lignite to Rs. 50 per 
tonne, but with prospective effect. The Neyveli Lignite Corporation was asked 
to pay to the Government of Tamil Nadu Rs.250 crores as a special 
dispensation against non-revision of royalty since 1993, which was recoverable 
from the royalty paid over the next thre e years. However, in March. 2001, by 
restoring parity for lignite to the levels of Grade V coal, as it was in 1991, the 
Government of India has not accounted fo r the revisions in royalty that were 
made much earlier for Grave V coal. If those rates are applied to lignite, 
Rs.541.29 crores is due to Tamil Nadu from 1990 to March 31, 2000. Hence, I 
request the Government to consider gi ving retrospective effect to royalty 
revisions for lignite on par with Grade V coal, and order release of Rs.54i.29  
crores, as arrears of royalty. Thank you, Madam.

diseases. The root-wilt disease is widesp read in eight Districts of the State,

issues are unlikely to be addressed, if the fundamental problem of improving

SHRI EDUAROO FALEIRO (Goa) : M adam, Deputy Chairman, over ' 
the last few decades, India had taken steps to become self-reliant in , armaments 
and established an R&D organisation and a Defence Industry to back it up.

with the wherewithal of Defence. -Yet, Madam, steps taken during the last 50

building nation. The proposal was to build  20 submarines at an approximate cost

finalised in 1997-98 by our Naval Submarine Design Bureau.

reported to cost the public excheque r a sum of Rs.12,500 crores for six 
SKD/CKD kits intended for assembly at Mazagon Docks, when the entiVe cost 
of the 20 submarines to be made under Project 75 India on both coasts was 
budgeted for Rs. 15,(300 crores, Govern ment must disclose the reasons for

Menace of ragging in the Country 
PROF, M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu) : Madam, Deputy 
Chairman, the menace of ragging has raised its ugly head yet again in New 
Delhi: I am sure that this is not confined to any particular college in New Delhi. 
It is a regular and recurring feature in innumerable colleges all over the 
country, where freshers are humiliated and tortured by the seniors. These 
incidents invariably end up in tragic incidents like some freshers committing 
suicide and in a recent incident, two freshers going deaf. 
Recently, the Supreme Court of I ndia has warned that if educational 
institutions fail to curb ragging, its affili ations to the universities and financial 
aid could be withdrawn. The Government should set high standards to be 
followed by the seniors in treating freshe rs and should issue st rict instructions 
to be followed by the colleges / educationa l institutions to monitor the seniors 
as to whether they are indulging in ragging with a view to harassing the 
freshers, which results in unwanted heartburn and unwarranted hatred among 
seniors and juniors. 
It is high time, the Government should ban 'ragging' in colleges / 
educational institutions so that freshers are relieved of ragging by seniors in 
future. Here, I would like to  stress that the senior students of the Santosh 
Medical College, Ghaziabad, whose alleged ragging which has led to two 
freshers going deaf should not be al lowed to go scot-free. Many a time, 
incidents of ragging by seniors go unnoticed or do not come to light. Because 
the freshers take the ragging by seniors lying down, these types of incident 
continue till another incident catches the headlines in the newspapers. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to bring forward a stringent 
legislation and take all necessary steps to put an end to these activities. once 
for all.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (g) A Statement

(a) and (d) A number of schemes and programmes are being 
implemented for manpower development in the field of rehabilitation and for 
providing service to the persons with disabilities through 6 National Institutes, 5 
Composite Rehabilitation centres, 4 Regional Rehabilitation Centres and 82 
District Disability Rehabilitation Centres. The Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment also supports over 800 Non-Governmental Organisations 
(NGOs) under the scheme to Promote Voluntary Action for Persons with 
Disabilities (Umbrella Scheme) and Assistance to Disabled for Purchase/Fitting of 
Aids and Appliances (ADIP). National Handicapped Finance Development Corporation 
(NHFDC) provides soft loan s for self-employment vent ures. Artificial Limbs 
Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO) is manufacturing and distributing 
various types of aids and appliances for persons with disabilities. The National 
Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism , Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation 
and Multiple Disabilities has came into being. Funds under these schemes and 
programmes are not allocated State-wise. 
(b) and (c) Scheme-wise utilization for the last three years and number of 
persons with disabilities benefited under the schemes are given in Statement-I 
{See below). State-wise release of funds for the Scheme to Promote Voluntary 
Action for Persons with Disabilities and Scheme of Assistane to Disabled Persons 
for Purchase/Fitting of Aids and Appliances is given in enclosed Statement-ll and 
III (See below) respectively. 
(e) to (g) Proposals to set up a College of Rehabilitation Sciences and a 
National Institute of Multiple Handicapped have been included in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan. Also the Ministry will continue to expand coverage under the Umbrella 
and ADIP schemes.

(a) to (c) As per the recruitment rule s for the post of Technicians, notified 
on 15th February, 1995, educational and other qualifications required for direct 
recruitment were Matriculation or equivalent and 
(i) A two year trade certificate from an ITI in Radio/TV Electronics/ 
Electrical or equivalent with one year practical experience after 
obtaining the certificate, or 
(ii) A one year trade certificate from an ITI in Air-conditioning and 
refrigeration with two years experience after obtaining the certificate. 
Prasar Bharati has informed that direct recruitment to the post of 
Technician is done by the Head of the Station concerned, who is the 
competent appointing authority in Prasar Bharati. It is possible that some Station 
Heads may have considered cadidates from recognised ITCs as eligible for the 
post. Information in this regard is being collected from about 500 stations. 
Fresh recruitment regulations governing, inter-alia, the post of 
Technician have been notified by Prasar Bharati, on 5th June, 2002, in 
accordance with Prasar Bharati Act, 1990. As per these regulations, the 
educational and other qualifications required for direct recruitment to the post of 
Technician, are Matriculation and at least 2 year diploma in 
Electronics/Telecommunications or equivalent from a recognized institute. 
However, on a call for strike given by the Joint Forum of Akashvani and 
Doordarshan Engineering Employees demanding, inter alia, their association 
in the process of framing of the rule s and regulations, the Prasar Bharati 
Management has, on 18th September, 2002, signed a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) with them, according to which, there would be 
comprehensive review of these rules and regulations.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a ) to (c) The Government has taken 
several measures to encourage Ayurvedic System of Medicine. These 
measures are:

quality assurance. Measures have been taken to address these issues.

However, Government have taken steps to augment supply of raw material. 
The Government have also projected t he need for conferring green industry 
and priority industry status to the IS M&H industry in its policy. These 
measures are expected to have positive effect on the cost of production and 
price of Ayurvedic products.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) No specific data is available on 
female foeticide as parties resort to this practice secretly in connivance with 
each other. The decrease in sex ratio from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001, in the 
age group of 0-6 years, leads to the co nclusion that female foeticide could be

To check the practice of female fo eticide on account of sex selection, 
the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (R egulation and Prevention of Misuse) 
Act, 1994 was brought into operation from 1st January, 1996 This Act prohibits 
determination and disclosure of sex of the foetus. The Act also prescribes 
punishments for contravening its provis ions with imprisonment upto 5 years 
and fine upto Rs. 50,000. 
Since the PNDT Act did not cover pre-conception selection and in order 
to ensure a more effective implementation of the Act, amendments have been 
placed on the Table of the Rajy a Sabha on 25.7.2002. Broadly, the 
amendments seek to: 
(i) bring the technique of pre-conception sex selection within the ambit of 
this Act to pre-empt its misuse;

1796. SHRI R.R GOENKA:

70 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Commission on Intellectual Property Rights 
appointed by the British Secretary of State, of which Dr. R.A. Mashelker was a 
Member, has submitted its report titled,  'Intellectual Property Rights and 
Development Policy; and 
(b) if so, the details of major recommendations contained in the report 
and Government's decision on each of them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) and (b) The Commission on Intellectual 
Property Rights was set up by the British Government with a view to consider 
(a) how national intellectual property regimes could best be designed to 
benefit developing countries within the context of international agreements, 
including the agreement on Trade Related Aspects of Intellectual Property; (b) 
how the international framework of rules and agreements might be improved 
and developed and (c) the broader policy framework needed to complement 
intellectual property regimes. Since the Commission was set up by the British 
Government, as such its Report has been submitted to the British Government 
on Septembers, 2002. 
It is, however, noted that the Repor t basically seeks to integrate 
intellectual property rights and development policy and, inter alia, emphasises 
the need for adequate sefeguards for de veloping countries. It is further noted 
that the main safeguards suggested in the Report in  respect of patent regime 
relate to: compulsory licensing; parallel imports; Government use of patent; 
exclusion of diagnostic, therapeutic an d surgical methods from patentability; 
exclusion of new uses of known products  from patentability; Bolar provision; 
prohibition of patent prot ection on plants and animals including genes and 
genetically modified plants and animals; and an obligation to disclose the 
geographical source of the genetic reso urces used in invention in the patent 
applications. The Patents Act, 1970 as amended by the Patents (Amendment) 
Act, 2002 substantially provides for thes e safeguards along with provisions 
which, in sum enable an appropriate timely and efficient response to national 
and public interest requirements/concerns.

Disinvestment of PSUs 
1821. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Disinvestment is meant to  strengthen private sector giants 
at the cost of public sector; 
(b) if not, why the public sector HPCL, BPCL and IPCL are being sold to 
private sector companies who naturally would be a powerful petroleum sector 
corporate; and 
(c) will it create a healthy competition? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) 
No, Sir. The object of disinvestment is to put national assets to optimal use and 
lo unleash the productive potential inherent in public sector 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2 002] 
enterprises. As per the declared policy of the Government on disinvestment, all non-
strategic PSUs can be disinvested, though the Government may continue the 
presence of public sector, as a countervailing force, where necessary, to prevent 
concentration of power in private hands. IPCL has already been disinvested on 
4th June, 2002. There is no evidence so far that the disinvestment has resulted in 
abuse of market dominance. With respect to BPCL and HPCL, Government had 
decided in February, 2002 in principle' to disinvest in these companies with the 
modalities to be worked out through consultations between the different 
Ministries concerned. Modalities will be worked out in the coming weeks.

crores as post-closure settlement of BALCO?

Sir. Financial bid of M/s Hindustan Lever Ltd. (HLL) for acquiring 74% 
Government equity in Modern Food Industries (India) Ltd. (MFIL) was based on 
the audited accounts of MFIL for the year ended 31 -3-1999. The Share Purchase 
Agreement between the Government and HLL was executed on 31-1-2000. It 
provided for post-closing adjustments in the following manner:— 
(i) If the Closing Date Net Working Capital Amount is greater than the 
1999 Net Working Capital Amount, the Purchaser shall pay the 
Government an amount equal to the difference between the 
Closing Date Net Working Capital Amount and the 1999 Net 
Working Capital Amount multiplied by 0.74. If the 1999 Net 
Working Capital Amount is greater than the closing Date Net 
Working Capital Account, the Government shall pay the Purchaser 
equal to the difference between the 1999 Net Working Capital 
Amount and the Closing Date Net Working Capital Amount 
multiplied by 0.74.

Price of Medicines 
1828. SHRIAIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the spiraling prices 
of medicines, which have gone beyond the reach of the common-man; 
(b) if so, whether the revised National Health Policy contemplates 
eradication of certain diseases over a de finite period of ti me and for effective 
control of others; 
(c) if so, the details of the programmes, disease-wise; and 
(d) the steps taken to keep the medicines required therefor within the 
reach of the average and poor patients? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) In the changing economy, revision of prices 
of medicines as in other commodities, is a normal feature. While the prices of 
some medicines increase, some others decrease. 
Under the provisions of the Drug (Prices Control) Order, 1995, the prices 
of 74 bulk drugs and the formulations containing any of these drugs are controlled. 
The Government/NPPA fixes/revises their prices from time to time as per formula 
provided under DPCO. In respect of drugs which are not covered under price 
control (non-scheduled formulations), the manufacturers ar e free to fix the 
prices by themselves without seeking approval of Government/NPPA. Such 
prices are normally fixed depending on various factors like the cost of bulk drugs 
used in the formulations, cost of excipients, cost of R&D, cost of 
utilities/packing materials, sales promotion cost, trade margins and quality 
assurance cost etc. 
The Government/NPPA regularly monitors the movement of prices of 
medicines of mass consumption marketed in trade channel and takes action 
whenever instances of unreasonable increase in prices affecting public interest 
adversely are noticed. 
In order to keep a watch on the pr ices of medicines marketed in the 
country, the NPPA regularly analyses the price trends in the market. An 
analyses of date (December, 1998-December-2001) of ORG-MARG, 
115 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
which publishes monthly report of "Retail Store Audit Market for 
Pharmaceutical Producers in India" revealed the following position with respect 
of prices of medicines having a minimum annual sale value of Rs. 1.00 crore: 
(i)   There were 2557 such medicines which existed during 1999 to 2001. 
(ii)  The prices of 54%, 51 % and 49% of the above medicines have gone up 
during the year 1999,2000 and 2001 respectively. 
(iii) the prices of 12%, 8% and 9% of the above medicines have 
decreased during the same period respectively. 
(iv) The prices of 34%, 41 % and 42% of the above medicines have 
remained same during the same period respectively. 
(b) and (c) The main objective of this policy is to achieve an acceptable 
standard of good health amongst the ge neral population of the country. The 
approach would be to increase access to the decentralized public health 
system by establishing new infrastructu re in deficient areas, and by upgrading 
the infrastructure in the existing instit utions. Overriding importance would be 
given to ensuring a more equitable access to health services across the social 
and geographical expanse of the country. Emphasis will be given to increasing 
the aggregate public health investment  through a substantially increased 
contribution by the Central Government. It is expected that this initiative will 
strengthen the capacity of the public health  administration at the State level to 
render effective service delivery. The contribution of the private sector in 
providing health services would be much enhanced, particularly for the 
population group which can afford to pay for services. Primacy will be given to 
preventive and first-line curative initiatives at the primary health level through 
increased sectoral share of allocation. Emphasis will be laid on rational use of 
drugs within the allopathic system. Increased access to tried and tested 
system of traditional medicine will be en sured. Within these broad objectives, 
NHP-2002 will endeavour to achieve the time-bound goals fo r eradication of 
the following diseases:—  
i.      Eradicate Polio and Yaw 2005 
ii.     Eliminate Leprosy 2005 
116 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA  
III. Eliminate Kala Azar 2010 
iv. Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis 2015 
v. Achieve Zero level growth of HIV/AIDS 2007 
vi. Reduce Mortality by 50% on account of TB, Malaria 
and other Vector and Water Borne diseases 
2010 
vii. Reduce Prevalence of Blindness to 0.5% 2010 
viii. Reduce IMR to 30/1000 and MMR to 100/Lakh 2010 
(d) In order to ensure availability of drugs at reasonable prices, the 
Government has been promulgating Drugs (Prices Control) Order under the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 from time to time. Medicines under the Disease 
Control Programmes are provided free of cost.

facilities under Government schemes to parents giving birth to third Child and also 
debar them from contesting any election like Panchayat and Municipal 
Corporation; and
