SHRI B.J. PANDA (Orissa): Mada m, the amendment to the seven-
year old Cable T.V. Act is going to have a far-reaching impact on more than 
four crore households which have cable T. V. today, the broadcasting industry, 
the cable operators, and, last but not the least, on the Government revenues. 
But at the core of this amendment, there is a simple principle, and that principle 
is consumer choice. Today, there are four crore households. Suppose there 
are five persons per household. We ar e talking about 20 crore or 200 million 
people who are affected by this. Simply. They do not have the choice of what 
they want to watch. Let us take a mom ent and dwell on this industry which is a 
little more than one decade old. In these eleven or twelve years, this industry 
has reached the staggering figur e of four crore househol ds. Just to put it in 
perspective, compare it with telephones. Telephones have been around for 
nearly a century in this country, and in all this time, they have reached four-
and-a-half crores. And in just 11 or 12 years, this industry has reached four 
crores! This is nothing short of st upendous, and this growth has been made 
possible by a combination of many factors. The broadcasters have to be given 
credit for this because they have invested  thousands of cror es of rupees in 
developing content, which has taken Indian content, in quantity and quality, up 
to world-class standards. Today, this cont ent is watched not just in these four 
crore households in India, but across the globe, in western countries, in 
Eastern Asia and Africa. I compliment, just as an hon. Member, earlier, 
complimented, one of the broadcasting co mpanies, which has today reduced 
its tariffs by 25 per cent, and I also urge other broadcasting companies to take 
a hint from them and take similar measures which would be a gesture of 
goodwill towards the Indian consumer. In all of this, the Government has had a 
very light touch, which, I think, has be en a boon and a bonus for this industry. 
Like the IT industry, which has grown rapidly with very little Government 
involvement, this industry also has grown. In fact, in the early years, there was 
no regulation, and in the year 1994, t he Government issued an ordinance, 
which was converted into an Act in 1995. Initially, for the first half of this 
decade of growth, this was a tremend ous boon foi the Indian consumers, 
because they were used to watching a very limited broadcasting content, and 
in the space of 3-4 years, they had th e choice of 20 or 30 channels, and the 
average cost, in about 1997-98, after 4-5 years of this development of the 
industry, was only about 100 rupees -- 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2002]  
if you take rural areas, it was about 50-60 rupees, and in urban areas, it was 
about 150 rupees. If you look at the fi gures around 1997-98, you had millions 
of customers already hooked up for 30 channels, already showing world class 
content, paying about 100 rupees. But this was never going to last because 
this boon for the Indian consumer was not in line with what was happening in 
the rest of the world. If you look at the world model, the business model for 
cable television, it is very stark. There are lots of channels all over the world. A 
majority of them are what are known as FTA, free-to-air, channels. The 
broadcasters get their revenues from advertising; they don't charge the cable 
operators and, in turn, the consumers ar e not charged by the cable operators. 
The cable operators charge the consumers only for their own infrastructure 
and operating cost, which is their distribut ion cost. All the channels available in 
India were free to air, and, that is wh y, the cable operators were charging only 
their own infrastructure cost and the Indian consumer could get, at only 100 
rupees, a large number of channels.  So, what has gone wrong? 
Just now, Shri Pradhan has pointed out, how these tariffs have risen. 
Let me give a stark figure here. The firs t pay channel was started with the very 
light sum of two rupees and fifty paise in the year 1996. That  was the only one 
pay channel till 1998. From 1998-99 onwards, most of the channels turned pay 
and the staggering figure is after this. After the Indian consumer enjoyed this 
great boon at a reasonable cost, from t he year 1999 till the year 2002, the 
increase in pay channel cost has been 1400 per cent. It has not been always a 
bad story. I was pointing out that for the fi rst five, six or seven years, it was a 
boon for the Indian consumer. But for the last three years, from 1999 to 2002, I 
don't think, any industry, anywhere in t he world, forget about India, had had 
1400 per cent price increase. I am no t blaming the broadcasters. Anybody, 
who creates world class content, has, in my opinion, the freedom to charge 
what he wants to. But, at the same time , the consumer has, and must have, a 
freedom of what he wants to buy and what he does not want to buy. Today, the 
Indian consumer does not have this fr eedom, and this is what this Amendment 
is all about. 
I want to give another stark figure. Today, the nufhber of channels 
has gone upto 150-160. But, if you take out the channels, which are not really 
relevant to India, like Chinese, Korean and Russian channels, the channels, 
which are largely watched, if you go by TAM figures, there is a stark figure.   
The ratio of the Indian viewership of pay channels to free 
226 

[10 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
channels is 55:45. That means 55 per cent  of what the Indian viewers watch in 
totality across the country, including urban and rural figures, are pay channels 
and 45 per cent are free channels. How does this compare with the world? Let 
me not compare with America or Japan or Western countries. I choose Brazil 
to compare because Brazil is somewhat similar to India. In fact, its socio-
economic status is slightly higher than that of India. In terms of disposable 
income and earning capacity, it is a larger country. In Brazil, today, in the year 
2002, the percentage of viewership of free channels is 72 per cent compared to 
only 45 per cent in India. This is where the crux of the issue lies. The consumer 
must have a choice. Now, I have heard figures, that somebody gets cable TV 
for rupees 100 and somebody gets for rupees 150. I am quite astounded 
because if you go by this article of the Hindustan Times of November 28, if you 
simply add the cost of the pay channels , it adds up to about rupees 160. Now, 
there is cost of infrastructure, distribut ion, etc. So, the only way anybody can 
get it at less than rupees 160 or even at rupees 160 is, if the cable operator is 
fudging his figures. Now, there are no heroes. There are villains all across the 
situation. There is only one victim, that is, the Indian consumer. Madam, 
actually, I am wrong. There are two victim s. The Government is also a victim. 
Some years ago, they have started an entertainment tax in many States across 
the country. In this year's National Budget, there is a service tax. But the 
collection from entertainment tax and the service tax is only a pittance. It is 
because of under-reporting by  the cable operat ors. There is a huge jack up of 
prices by the broadcasters. But the cons umers don't have any choice.   Either 
they have to take it all or leave it all. 
Let me give one example to dramatise this choice. We all buy 
newspapers. This community, the Members of Parliament, is, probably, more 
interested in news. We all buy more newspapers than an average Indian family 
do. For example, at my house, I get fi ve or six newspapers every morning and 
I pay for each of them separately. My co lleague, Mr. Shukla, is saying that he 
takes 10 newspapers. But an average Indian household, I am quite confident, 
takes one or, at the most, two newspapers. We all buy newspapers according 
to what we need, what we can afford and what we want. How would it be, if 
there was a situation in the country where everybody had to take 60 
newspapers, and the cost should be averaged? My driver and assistant would 
pay the same amount as I do, whether they take one newspaper or 60 
newspapers. That is the situation toda y.   How would it be, if one publishing 
house, which has 30 or 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2002]  
40 publications, says, "You take all my publications or you don't have any of 
my publications"? I don't want to blam e anybody here. The broadcasters are 
within their right to charge what they wish. But we must ensure that the Indian 
consumer has the right and the physical option of taking or buying what he can 
afford and wishes to have. At the same ti me, we must also ensure that nobody 
is deprived of this television revolution that is taking place. 
This proposal provides that we follow the international model. It is 
true that internationally it is not al ways mandated. The Conditional Access 
System is often done by the market itself. The market, the broadcasters and 
the distributors, that is, the cable operators, work in tandem. They work as 
partners, and yet the consumers do not get  affected in those countries. In our 
country, it is a strange situation where t he vendors of the c ontent, that is, the 
broadcasters, and the distributors of  the content are at loggerheads. Though 
they are at loggerheads, they are not suffering. They are all doing well. It is the 
consumer who is suffering. We must not permit it to happen. 
We have talked about technology. We have talked about analogue 
versus digital costs. Madam, I want to  say something here. This amendment, 
at the core of it, is not about te chnology. Technology will come and go. 
Technology will keep changing. The core of it is a principl e that the Indian 
consumer, the Indian citizen, must have a choice. Now, the market should 
have allowed this to happen. The market has worked well in other countries. 
Unfortunately,, in our country, in this ma rket, it has not worked. It is a very odd 
situation. My hon. friend from West B engal is saying that he is normally not a 
votary of markets, but yet, on this iss ue, he supports the markets. It is an odd 
situation. I am normally a votary of markets. Yet, I am supporting the motion 
for Government intervention, because the market has failed. We, all of us, 
have supported Government intervention, when the market has failed. When 
there is a failure in the stock market, we insist on Government intervention. 
Then, why should' we no support Govern ment intervention, when there is a 
failure in this market? Perhaps, this industry has grown rapidly. It is an 
immature industry. It is hardly 11 years old. Perhaps, that is why the purveyors 
of the content and the dist ributors of the content h^ve not yet worked out a 
proper market relationship and that is wh y they are in conflict. That is why the 
Government needs to step in and mandate the consumer choice.    But, 
228 

[10 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
I urge upon the hon. Minister, let us exercise restraint. Let us not use this 
opportunity to go in for and mandate Government intervention for a long 
period. Whenever the Government tried to mandate technology, it has been a 
failure, not only in this country but also in other countries. We should not be 
mandating technology. We should not be really mandating prices. We should 
be mandating in this issue, the consumer choice. What will this do? This will 
put the Indian cable TV market on a par with the world situation, where the 
consumer will have an access to, say, 30 or 40 channels, consisting of all 
genre or all categories. A point was rais ed that the Government was going to 
get undue powers to dictate who could watch and what. That is not true. 
Please read the amendment. The amendment says that the Government can 
stipulate the categories, which it has a right to do. It can stipulate, for example, 
that adult content will not be shown. It can stipulate that only news content 
must be shown. But it cannot say "show Star News or do not show Zee News". 
That is not permitted in this amendment. So, let us be clear about this. Madam, 
I do not want to take too much time. Some speakers have pointed out some 
so-called shortcomings. I would like to say that let us not, in anticipation of the 
perfect, delay the good. 
This has been delayed for too long. So, I compliment the hon. 
Minister on standing up to the tremendo us odds in bringing this amendment 
before the House for passage, even though it is so many months since it was 
passed by the Lok Sabha. Once again, I would like to compliment her, and 
while supporting her, I would like to urge the community of this industry, both 
the broadcasters and the cabl e operators, to realise that if they do not self 
regulate themselves, the Government is bound to step in.

Madam, for the reasons unknown to us, this Bill was delayed for long.

passing of the Bill by the Lok Sabha, it is being discussed here. 
Madam, this Cable TV Networks Re gulation (Amendment) Bill, 2002, 
seeks to amend the original Act of 1995 by introducing a new provision, new 
Section 4A. By virtue of the new pr oposed amendments, Section 4(A), the 
Central Government or the Government  of India is getting the power to 
intervene in the fight between the br oadcasting houses or the broadcasting 
companies and the cable network compan ies. One side is the broadcasting or 
the production sector and the other is the distribution sector. It is an admitted 
fact that the quarrel or controversy is between them. The broadcasting houses 
are alleging that the actual number of connections which are being given by the 
cable network or the network agencies are not being disclosed, and that the 
broadcasting houses are being cheated.  This is the allegation of the 
broadcasting houses. The allegation of t he cable network agencies is that they 
are not having sufficient number of co nnections and they are being over-
charged by the broadcasting houses. So, who is being benefited out of this 
controversy, quarrel, or difference of opinion between these two? In fact, what 
is happening is, the poor Indian consumer is being cheated, as rightly said by 
Mr. Panda. So, the poor consumer, the In dian consumer, should be benefited 
by this provision. To that extent, I fully support this Bill because, today the 
consumer is being cheated because of this controversy. 
As pointed out by Dr. Subbarami Redd y, what is the real fact behind 
this controversy is still unknown. Why it is being dragged on for a long time is 
still unknown to the House. So, considerin g the fact that there are forty million 
viewers of Cable TV, definitely, the Go vernment of India should have the 
control on this.  This is my first submission. 
Now, coming to the other points, I would say that even after the 
passing of the Bill, the cable TV operat or is> going to have the domain to 
declare the number of connections, becau se he has to declare the number of 
connections to the Government of India.  So, it means still the domain is with 
him or he is having the authority. I would like to seek a clarification from the 
hon. Minister as to how it will be supe rvised or checked. Madam, the estimated 
value of a STB or of an addressable system which has to be

THE BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY BILL, 2002 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): I beg to move: 
"That the Bill to provide for conservation of Biological Diversity, 
sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of 
the benefits arising out of  the use of biological resources, knowledge 
and for matters connected therewith or  incidental thereto, as passed 
by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, I have the proud privilege of introducing the motion for 
consideration of a Bill which aims at regulating the access to and conservation 
of our rich and diverse eco-systems.  This Bill has been unanimously passed 
by the Lok Sabha. 
Biodiversity, the variety of life on earth, is the backbone for any 
country's ecological security and livelihood security of its people. It constitutes 
the resources upon which human beings, communities, nations and future 
generations depend. 
254 

[10 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
In the past, the biological resource s of the country and associated 
traditional knowledge have been shared freely with other countries, regarding 
biodiversity as a common heritage of humanity. But, after the entry into force 
of the United Nations' Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), to which India 
is a party, this scenario has changed. 
The CBD, while affirming the principl e of sovereign rights of States 
over their own biological resources, enjoins upon the contracting parties to 
facilitate access to genetic resources by other parties through national 
legislation and/or regulations. The recipient is required to provide fair and 
equitable sharing of benefits arising from the use of genetic resources 
transferred. 
In this background, we have developed the Biological Diversity 
legislation. I am happy to inform this august House that we are one of the very 
few countries in the world, and the first among the 12 Megadiversity nations, 
to develop such a legislation. ...(Interruptions)... 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Excuse me 
Mr. Minister. I think, too many people ar e talking. I cannot even hear what the 
Minister is saying. ...(Interruptbns)... 
SHRI T.R. BAALU: The legislatio n primarily addresses the issue 
concerning access to genetic resources and associated knowledge by foreign 
individuals, institutions or companies, and equitable sharing of benefits arising 
out of the use of these resources and knowledge with the country and the 
people. 
I am thankful to the Standing Commi ttee, which is chaired by the 
hon. Member Shri Ramachandraiah, for the in-depth consideration of the Bill 
and valuable recommendations. 
As the Biological Diversity Bill provides for checking biopiracy and 
realising equitable sharing of benefits aris ing out of the utilisation of our rich 
biological resources and associated traditional knowledge, I appeal for 
support from all sections of this House. 
With these words, Sir, I commend the Bill to the House. 
Thank you. 
The questbn was proposed.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Atrocities against Dalits In Haryana, Bihar and other parts of the Country 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): Sir, hon. Member s of Rajya Sabha raised the issue 
regarding killing of five members of Scheduled Castes in Dulina in Jhajjar 
District of Haryana.   I am, accordingly, making a statement on the incident. 
The facts of the case, as reported by  the Government of Haryana, are 
that on 15 th October, 2002, on the Dussehra Day, five persons were coming 
from Farukh Nagar, District Gurgaon, and were going to Karnal. They were 
carrying 228 hides (34 hides of cows, 2 hides of she;ep and 192 hides of 
buffaloes) and a dead cow in a TATA 407 vehicle. While going to Karnal from 
Farukh Nagar, they crossed police post Dulina and stopped between Dulina 
and Jhajjar. They started removing the skin of the dead cow along the road 
side. It was around 6.30 p.m. and th e people of adjoining villages were 
returning home after attending Dussehera celebrations in Jhajjar town. Seeing 
the deceased persons skinning the cow, public thought that cow slaughter was 
being carried out openly. About 50-60 persons gathered there and gave severe 
beating to all the five deceased pers ons. The public took the deceased to 
Police Post Dulina where they reporte d that the deceased were carrying out 
cow slaughter on which the Assistant Sub-Inspector registered a case No. 469 
under section 3/8 Punjab Prohibition of Cow Slaughter Act, 1955 against all the 
deceased persons. However, ASI after making preliminary enquiry told the 
public that it was not a case of cow slaughter, instead a dead cow was bought 
by the deceased from Farukh Nagar and was being skinned but the villagers 
strongly argued with the Assistant Sub- Inspector of Police and it was decided 
that verification be done from Farukh Nagar whether the cow was bought dead 
or alive. Team consisting of head Constable, driver of the vehicle Tata 407 and 
one person from the public was sent to Farukh Nagar. On verification, it was 
established that the cow was bought  dead by the deceased persons. The 
verification party came back to Dulina at about 8.00 p.m. by which time many 
passers-by saw the half-skinned cow an d the rumour about cow slaughter 
spread in Jhajjar town and nearby villages. People in thousands armed with 
lathi, jaily etc. gathered there and blocked 
260 

[10 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
the main road. On hearing this Dy. Supdt. Of Police, Jhajjar, SHO, Jhajjar 
alongwith force, Naib Tehsildaar, Jhajjar and City magistrate, Jhajjar also 
reached the spot. However, the mob swelled further and became violent. They 
started pelting stones on the police perso nnel. Many police and civil officers 
received injuries. They tried to pacify them but they did not listen to the 
reason. The police resorted to lathi charge  but that was also of no avail. The 
mob set on fire the TATA 407 vehicle and a hut near the Police Post. They 
tried to set the police post also on fire. 
The mob out-numbered the police and it was already dark. The 
Magistrates and the police officers present on the spot decided not to resort to 
firing as the situation would further worsen because there was no space left 
between the mob and the police and they were surrounded by the mob from 
all sides. Suddenly a violent group of hooligans armed with iron rods and other 
deadly weapons reached there and pushed the police personnel and 
magistrates aside and broke open the do or of the police post. They attacked 
all the five alleged cow slaughterers with iron rods, lathis, stones and brick-
bats etc. and took them out on the main road. There, they beat them to death. 
They threw two dead bodies in the hut which was already on fire. 
A case No.  470 dated i5.IO.2OO2 u/S 148/149/302/435/332/353/452 
IPC dated 15.10.2002 was registered in connection with the incident. A 
Special Investigation Team consisting of DSP Jhajjar, Inspector, Bahadurgarh, 
SI and SHO Jhajjar and ASI in charge of Police Post, Dulina was constituted 
to conduct the investigation. The post -mortem of the dead bodies was got 
done by a board of doctors and the de ad bodies were handed over to the 
relatives of the deceased. Post-mortem  of the cow was also conducted in 
which it was established that the cow died at least 24 hours before the 
incident. During the investigation, 24 accused persons have been arrested so 
far and section 3(2) of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of 
Atrocities) Act, 1989 has been added. 
The Government of Haryana also ordered an enguiry by Divisional 
Commissioner, Rohtak into the whole incident. The Government of Haryana 
has announced ex-gratia relief of Rs.5 lakh to next of the kin of each deceased 
and the amount has been paid. Government has also promised job to one of 
the members of the family of each deceased person. 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2002]  
The Divisional Commissioner, Rohtak completed inquiry and 
submitted his report on 5th December, 2002. The Government of Haryana have 
examined the report and accepted the same in toto. The Commissioner in his 
report has found that the Police personnel did not take adequate steps to save 
the five innocent persons who were in their lawful custody. The Executive 
Magistrate and other administrative o fficers also did not perform their duty 
properly, as a result of which this unfor tunate incident took place. Keeping in 
view the report of the Enquiry Officer,  the State Governm ent has decided to 
take action against all erring-officers and officials who were deputed for 
controlling the situation. They are being charge-sheeted for major penalty. 
Haryana has a history of communal harmony since ages. People of all 
sections of society live in peace and harmony. Crime against SC/ST is taken 
seriously and investigated by a Gazetted officer. In fact, it appears that the 
incident took place because of the mist aken impression that a cow slaughter 
was being committed openly which aroused the passions of the people and it 
should not be treated as a deliberate atrocity committed on the members of the 
Scheduled Caste. 
So far as atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes in Bihar 
and other parts of the country are c oncerned, no major incident has been 
reported in the recent past. In fact, there has been a perceptible decline in the 
IPC crimes committed against Scheduled Ca stes in the last 5 years. While 
18,658 IPG crimes were committed in 1997, this number came down to 17,397 
in 2000 which shows a decline of 6.8%. As regards incidence of crime under 
the Protection of Civil Rights Act. 1955. there was a decline of 78% from 3683 
in 1990 to 810 in 2000. Similarly, the incidence of crime under Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 showed a 
decline of 13.4% from 17,511 in 1995 to 15,157 in 2000. 
The Ministry of Home Affairs have been issuing guidelines to the State 
Governments from time to time to give more focused attention to improving the 
administration of the crimin al justice system to ensur e prevention of atrocities 
against SCs, STs, women and other vu lnerable sections of society. The 
guidelines issued by MHA include, inter-alia, the sensitisation of police 
personnel in the implementation of the Protec tion of Civil   Rights   Act,   1955   
and   the   Scheduled   Castes/  Scheduled   Tribes 
262 

[10 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, instru ctions to the police  to have a more 
empathetic approach while dealing with t he cases of atrocities against them, 
specifying the scope and responsibility of  the police personnel investigating 
such offences, recruitment of sufficient  number of persons belonging to SCs/ 
STs/minorities as police personnel, especially, at the cutting edge level, setting 
up of special cells to deal with such offences, programmes for creating 
awareness among the vulnerable sections of society and legal recourse open 
to them, evaluation of the working of s pecial courts, identification of atrocity-
prone areas for prevention of crime and measures to be taken for economic 
and social rehabilitation of the victims of atrocities.

(c) to (e) A Fly Ash Mission was set up in 1994 promote the utilization of fly 
ash in the country by generating confidence in user agencies regarding feasible 
modes of utilization of fly ash in the country. The Mission has been playing a 
useful catalytic role in increasing the utilization of fly ash in the country. 
Ministry of Environment & Forests (MOEF) have issued a Gazette 
Notification dated 14.09.1999 regarding utilization of fly ash. The 
Notification, inter-alia, requires 100% utilization of fly ash for all new power 
plants within 9 years as well as 100% use of fly ash for all existing power plants 
within 15 years. The Notification enjoins upon the thermal power plants to 
draw up the action plan for utilization/disposal of the fly ash. 
At present, about 19 Million Tonne of fly ash constituting 22% of the 
fly ash produced in the country is being utilized. This has increased from 2.739 
Million Tonne of fly ash constituting about 6.61 % in 1995-96.

Modernisation of NSG 
*310. SHRIK. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the sanctioned strength of National Security Guards (NSG) and the 
number of vacant posts as on 1 st July, 2002; and 
(b) what steps have been taken to modernise the force, increase its 
sanctioned strength and fill up the vacant posts, in view of the increased role of 
the NSG in the present context? 
THE DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, INCHARGE OFTHE MINISTRY 
OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
NSG was raised as a contingency deployment force to deal with terrorist 
activities in various states and anti-hijacking operations. The force is trained and 
equipped to meet these challenges. 
NSG is a 100% deputationist force drawing personnel from the Army, 
Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs) and other Police Organisations. The 
sanctioned strength of NSG is 7330 personnel. There were 1202 vacant posts 
as on 1st July, 2002. The Army, CPMFs and other Police Organisations have 
been advised to sponsor adequate number of personnel to fill up the vacant posts. 
The recent enhancement of NSG allowance is expected to reduce the level of 
vacancies. 
A modernisation plan entailing total expenditure of Rs. 82.49 crores over a 
period of 5 years commencing from the year 2002-03 has been approved for 
NSG. Out of this, Rs. 14.83 crores have been sanctioned during the current 
financial year. 
No change in the role of NSG or increase in its sanctioned strength is 
contemplated at present.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Wil the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that power shortage in peak as well as general hours

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The transmission and distribution (T&D) losses in the 
developed countries of the world are in the range of 6-11%. The level of T&D 
losses in the country is around 31% and is higher than that of the developed 
countries of the world. While the losses in Extra High Voltage network (EHV) 
about 4-5% bulk of the losses occur in the sub-transmission and distribution 
systems. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
The reasons for high T&D losses in the country are on account of: 
i. weak and inadequate sub-transmission and distribution system due to 
low priority being given to these works 
ii. large scale rural electrification programme undertaken in the 
country resulting in long lines and extension of distribution 
network without strengthening the back-up transmission and sub-
transmission system 
iii. too many transformation stages resulting in higher component of 
transformation losses 
iv. improper load management resulting in over loading of system 
v. lower power factor due to pumping load in rural areas, and air 
conditioners, coolers and industrial loads in urban areas and 
inadequate reactive compensation at the load points 
vi. low quality of construction and inadequate maintenance of 
equipment 
vii. unmetered supply to agricultural pumps and small domestic 
connections to weaker sections of the society in some states 
viii. pilferage and theft of energy. 
In order to achieve commercial viability, Ministry of Power has 
formulated a six level intervention strategy that encompasses initiatives at 
national level, state level, SEB/Utility level, distribution circle level, feeder 
level and the consumer level. This six level intervention strategy will focus on 
accountability, deliverability and performance at all levels to rejuvenate the 
distribution sector, where the maximum interface with the ultimate customers 
exists, the highest value addition occurs, and eighty percent of total T&D 
losses including nearly all the commercial losses take place. 
To give a strong impetus to the process of reforms, the Ministry of Power 
organized a Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers on Power Sector 
Reforms on 3rd March 2001. It was emphasised inter alia that commercial 
viability has to be achieved in distribution in 2-3 years through any or all of the 
following 
— Creating profit centres with full accountability 
— Handing over local distribution to Panchayats/Local Bodies/ 
Franchisees/Users Association, wherever necessary 
38 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
— Privatisation of distribution 
25 States have signed Memorandum of Understanding for undertaking 
reforms and restructuring in a time bound manner and linking the support of 
Government of India to achievement of predetermined milestones.To bring 
about commitment towards distribution reforms, State Electricity Boards/Utilities 
have been asked to sign a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with Ministry of 
Power as a pre-requisite for release of Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme (APDRP) funds. Till now 18 States have signed the MoA. A 
number of States have enacted anti-electricity theft legislation. 
To reduce the transmission and distribution losses in a phased manner, 
the Government of India has launched the APDRP in February 2000.The 
APDRP includes upgradation of sub-transmission and distribution network, energy 
audit activities and metering in a phased manner.

fire agreements with the National Socialist Council of Nagaland (NSCN) (IM 
faction) on 25th July 1997 and with the NSCN (K. faction) on 28th April, 2001.

Action regarding streamlining madarsas functioning in India 
2140. SHRINANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the light of Pakistan clamping down on all the Madarsas of 
Pakistan and binding on them to fall in line with mainstream of Education, to curb 
militancy and to curb the flow of foreign funds to them; has our Government 
taken any steps so far to streamline Madarsas functioning to curb I.S.I, and 
foreign funds flowing into them; 
(b) if so, the details of action taken so far; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) Madarsa is a traditional institution for religious 
education. Its regulation is primarily the concern of the State Governments. 
Relevant laws already exist to curb militancy and the law enforcing agencies keep a 
close watch on the activities of all fundamentalist organisations and institutions 
having a bearing on communal harmony and internal security and take appropriate 
action wherever necessary. 
So far as the flow of foreign funds into Madarsas is concerned, under 
the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 various NGOs (including 
Madarsas) in India are permitted to recei ve foreign contribution from foreign 
sources for bona-fide activities in cultural, economic, educational, social or 
religious fields. Permission under the aforesaid Act is given only after careful 
verification of their antecedents. Funds which come through these source follow 
legal banking channels and are open to scrutiny and inspection. If any complaint 
of violation of the provisions of this Act comes to notice of the Government, 
appropriate action is taken under the law.

(c) "Police" is a State subject as per the Constitution of India and 
therefore it is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments to

security and law and order scenario, particularly in the face of growing 
terrorism and organized criminal activiti es, the Ministry of Home Affairs has 
been supplementing the efforts of the State Governments in modernizing their 
police forces by way of implementing a Scheme for Modernization of State 
Police Forces since 1969-70,under which financial assistance is extended to 
State Governments for purchased weaponry, communication equipment,

capacity, mixed traffic conditions, over-speeding, over-loading, drunken

electricity within a State is in the purview of concerned State Government/ Power 
Utility, and the instant case, it is Government of NCT Delhi/Delhi TRANSCO

privatization of electricity distribution in Delhi i.e. w.e.f. 1st July, 2002 is

95

(c) and (d) In order to improve the power situation in Delhi, following steps 
are being taken by Delhi TRANSCO LtdVDelhi Generation Company/ Distribution 
Companies" : 
(i) Augumentation of transmission and distribution system at all 
voltage levels commensurate with load growth in the concerned areas. 
(ii) Action Plan for strengthening of T&D system during 10th Plan has 
already been prepared and the work is being carried out. 
(iii) Pragati Power Project is nearing completion which will provide 330 
MW power to Delhi.

is taking following steps to augment availability of power and thereby mitigate

network of the state system for reduction in T&D losses and 
improving quality in power supply. Project schemes aggregating Rs. 
946.46 crores have been approved under Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for 
upgradation/augmentation of sub-transmission and distribution system 
in Delhi.

generation capacity of 7340 MW is planned during 10th Plan 
period in the Central Sector in the Northern region in which

(iii) Establishment/Strengthening of inter-regional transmission links for 
enhancement of inter-state and inter-regional transfer of

country. Already, 220 KV Sasaram back-to-back project has been 
commissioned which has enabled flow of surplus power from

conservation measures.

2155. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that 9953 villages in Orissa are yet to 
be electrified; 
(b) if so, the number of villages in Orissa to be electrified during the

the villages in Orissa? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) As per Central Electricity Authority 
(CEA) statistics, there are 46989 inhabited villages in Orissa (1991 census). Of 
these, 35232 villages have been declared as electrified as on 30th April, 2001

(b) Planning Commission has allocated an amount of Rs. 108.63

the rate of 6 lakhs. Government has drawn the attention of Orissa

electrification programme during the current financial year at least to the 
extent of allocation made in the year 2001 -02 which stood at Rs. 17.04 
crores.

schemes are determined by the State Governments/State Electricity 
Boards/Power Utilities based on the directions and policies of the State 
Governments' concerned. However, in the Chief Ministers'conference held 
on 3rd March, 2001, it was resolved to complete electrification of all villages 
by 2007 and achieve coverage of all household by 2012.

and Rs. 11.33 crores under Minimum Needs Programme (MNP) to the Government

Government has released an amount of Rs. 30.00 crores to Orissa. 
  States can also access funds from Rural Electrification Corporation 
(REC), Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) and Member of 
Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) for the programme. 
  Rural Electrification Corporation have formulated new schemes for 
electrification of dalit bastis and hamlets at lower rate of interest.

year-wise for completing the electrification of all villages during the 10th Plan.

(b) how many of these new companies/corporations have started earning 
profits or have reached break-even; 
(c) the Revenue Receipts of these companies during last 12 months and 
how does these compare with the Receipts of same period in the previous 
years; and 
(d) the remedies available to the consumer for redressal of grievance related 
with deficiency in service against these private companies or corporations 
etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) to (c) There is a general consensus 
among all States on the need for power sector reforms. In the Conference of Chief 
Ministers/Power Ministers held in March 2001. It was agreed that there is an 
urgent need to depoliticise power sector reforms and speed up their 
implementation. It was also recognized that the real challenge of reforms lies 
in distribution sector and that commercial viability has to be achieved in 
distribution through any or all of the following: 
— Creating Profit Centres with full accountability. 
— Handing over of local distribution to Panchayats/Local Bodies/ 
Franchisees/Users Associations, wherever necessary. 
— Privatisation of distribution. 
— Or any other means. 
Eight States (Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi) have undertaken reforms 
by enacting their own Reform Laws which provide, inter-alia, for 
unbunding/corporatisation of SEBs. Distribution has been privatized in Orissa 
and Delhi. 
The reform measures including unbundling of SEBs, were undertaken by 
these States at a time when the financial health of the sector was very 
104 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
poor. The corporations/companies created as a result of reorganization of SEBs 
have shown improvements on various fronts including metering supply of 
electricity, increase in billing and collection efficiency etc. 
The distribution in Orissa was privatized in 1999 when the 
Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses were very high, the billing and 
collection efficiency was very poor, the status of metering was not 
encouraging. Consequent on privatisation of distribution, signs of 
improvement on these and other operational levels are visible. The process of 
restructuring of electricity industry including privatisation of distribution in 
Orissa was reviewed by the State Government and it was decided that the 
upvaluation of the assets of the erstwhile State Electricity Board (SEB) may be 
kept in abeyance as it was resulting in increase in the cost of power and 
making it difficult for the sector to achieve commercial viability. 
In Delhi distribution has been privatized recently in July, 2002. Prior to 
privatisation the Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) loss levels as 
approved by the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) for the 3 
distribution zones taken together were at 50.7%. It is too early to assess the 
performance of these private companies in Delhi. 
(d) As per the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998, the 
Regulatory Commissions have the mandate to inter-alia, safeguard the interest 
of the consumers. The Electricity Bill, 2001 which has been introduced in 
Lok Sabha and is presently under consideration by the Standing Committee 
on Energy makes specific provisions on consumer protection, empowering the 
Regulatory Commissions to specify performance standards of distribution 
licensees. Failure to meet the standards makes the licensees liable for payment 
of compensation to the affected person.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) With a view to providing an 
impetus to R&D efforts in the Power Sector, a Standing Committee on R&D 
was set up under the Chairman, Central Electricity Authority with Director 
General, Central Power Research Institute as Member Convener. It has prepared a 
perspective research and development plan for the next 15 years in order to 
ensure optimum utilization of the research and development infrastructure by 
establishing linkage between: 
a. The basic and the applied research and development needs of 
the power sector; 
b. The national level £;)d organizational level research and 
development plans; 
to channelise the outcome of research for the benefit to the customers and the 
operational efficiency of the power sector. 
The R&D Perspective Plan identifies and prioritizes the crucial R&D needs 
required to bridge the technology gaps in various subsections of power sector 
(Generation, Transmission & Distributio n). In addition, the following policy 
issues are adui essed which are essential for formulating strategies and further 
successful implementation. 
 Need for a Nodal R&D agency to formulate strategic plans and 
partnerships. 
 Networking and Mapping the R&D resources including 
intellectual capital. 
 Strengthening the existing R&D infrastructure. 
  Nurturing the R&D human resources. 
 Funding for R&D initiatives.

Corruption in Watershed Programmes 
2173. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Watershed Programmes 
undertaken by NGOs in various parts of the country are steeped in corruption, 
in the absence of any physical audits; 
(b) if so, the facts and details thereof; 
(c) whether the grants for Watershed Programmes given by the Union 
Government to NGOs have been siphoned off; 
(d) if so, whether any physical verification of proper use of grants have 
been undertaken by Government; and 
(e) if not.the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) to (e) The Ministry of 
Rural Development is administering three major Watershed Development 
Programmes, namely, the Integrated Wastelands Development Programme, Desert 
Development Programme and Drought Prone Areas Programme. Central funds 
for implementation of these Programmes by the State Governments are 
released directly to the concerned District Rural Development Agencies 
(DRDAs)/Zilla Parishads (ZPs).They, in turn, make releases to the Project 
Implementation Agencies (PIAs), which may also include NGOs among others. 
The identification and appointment of NGOs for implementation of these 
Watershed Projects is to be done by DRDAs/ ZPs. After release of the first 
instalment of Central funds along with the Sanction Order to the Watershed 
Projects, subsequent instalments are 
119 

RAJYA SABHA             [11 December, 2002] 
released only after ascertaining that the funds earlier released had been 
properly utilized for the purpose they were meant, through Utilisation 
Certificates, Audited Statement of Accounts, Project Action Plan etc. In 
addition, after a Watershed Project received 45% of the Project cost, it is 
mandatory that a Mid-Term Evaluation of the Project gets conducted by an 
independent evaluator. The next instalment to the Project is released only 
when the Evaluation Report clearly indicates satisfactory performance of the 
Project and utilization of funds as per the approved work plan. 
In the case of Watershed Projects implemented through NGOs by the 
Council of Advancement of People's Action and Rural Technology 
(CAPART), there is a system of physical audit of its programmes in the form 
of a three-tier monitoring system by independent monitors viz., pre-funding 
appraisal before sanctioning a project, mid-term evaluation during the 
implementation of the project and post evaluation after completion of the 
project. This system adopted by CAPART has prevented misuse of funds for 
the programmes.

Problem of the Handloom and Powerloom Sectors in the country 
2197. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the problems being faced by handloom and powerloom sectors in the 
country; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to solve these problems; and 
(c) how the handloom and powerloom sectors workers are benefited by 
Government's policies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OFTEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) The main problems faced by the Handloom 
sector have been traditional production technique and low level of technology 
and skills, lack of modernization and Research and Development efforts, lack 
of adequate and timely supply of inputs like yarn, dyes & chemicals, non-
availability of adequate and timely credit facilities on concessional rate of 
interest. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, the problems being faced are 
technological obsolescence, small size of units with fragmentation, lack of 
credit availability, poor marketability, low level of skill and poor quality 
consciousness. 
(b) Looking into various problems being faced by the handloom sector, the 
Government have been implementing various schemes for the promotion and 
development of the handloom sector.The schemes include Development of 
Exportable Products and their Marketing, conducting Expos and Fairs, 
Welfare Schemes viz. Workshed-cum-Housing, Health Package, Group 
Insurance, Thrift Fund and New Insurance etc. A new Scheme, namely Deen 
Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana has also been introduced in 2000-2001 to 
cover entire gamut of activities from basic inputs and working capital to 
provisions of design, marketing, publicity etc. Apart from this, Government 
has set up National Centre for Textile Design (NCTD) to collate and disseminate 
all information related to textile weave, fabric, colour, design etc. to act as an 
electronic and regular forum to give the weavers design and marketing 
exposure. The Government has also promulgated the Handloom (Reservation of 
Articles for Production) Act, 1985 under which at present 11 categories of 
textile articles are exclusively reserved for production on handlooms. 
144 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
In order to give continued protection to the handloom weavers, the 
State Governments have been instructed to arrange distribution of hank yarn 
to handloom weavers, free of excise duty (CENVAT) through designated 
organizations which could claim reimbursement of the incidence of CENVAT 
borne by them on such yarn from the Government of India. 
The Hon'ble Prime Minister had also announced in his address to the 
nation on August 15, 2002, the facility of a one time special rebate @ 10% of 
the value of the handloom products sold, so as to enable the handloom sector 
to dispose of their stock and kick-start this employment intensive industry by 
reviving its production cycle. For this, a sum of Rs. 100 crore was 
announced.The State Governments have already been instructed to take 
advantage of this rebate and prefer their claims for reimbursement of the 
rebate amounts. The Prime Minister had also announced a scheme with an 
outlay of Rs.125 crore, for imparting training to 1 lakh weavers/artisans so as 
to enhance their skill and marketing/ managerial capabilities. Further, a 
special contributory insurance scheme for 1 Million weavers/artisans 
combining the Jan Shree Bima Yojana of the Life Insurance Corporation of 
India with Group Insurance was also announced. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, the Government has initiated 
a programme of modernization with induction of 50,000 shuttleless looms, 
and of 2.5 lakh semi-automatic and automatic looms in the decentralized 
powerloom sector. The TUFS has been modified so that the small-scale 
textile sector including the powerloom sector has been given an option for 
either 12% Upfront Credit Linked Capital Subsidy or the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
The Government has also undertaken modernization and upgradation of 
Powerloom Service Centres (PSC), by providing upgraded equipment and 
Computer Aided Design (CAD) facility. The Government has also accepted 
the recommendations of a three-member committee of the Ministry of 
Textiles, for streamlining of management and supervision of PSCs, providing 
infrastructure and enhanced grant in aid. 
Welfare measures such as the Group Insurance Scheme and Worksheds 
have also been initiated. 
(c) As a result of the various measures taken, the handloom sector, 
which provides employment to about 124 lakh persons engaged in weaving 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
and other allied activities, has been able to register a ten-fold increase in 
production of fabrics from a level of 500 million sq. metres in the early 50s to 7586 
million Sq. metres in 2001-2002. This sector contributes to nearly 19% of the 
total cloth produced in the country. Exports of cotton handloom fabrics and made-
ups which were of the value of Rs.1840 crore during the year 1997-98, increased to 
Rs.2065 crore during the year 2001 -02. During the period April-July, 2002, 
exports were of Rs.851.93 crore as against Rs.667.53 crore during April-July, 
2001. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, it plays an important role in the 
economy of the country providing employment to about 417.9 lakh weavers. The 
number of powerlooms has grown to an estimated figure of 16.71 lakh as on 
30.08.2002. This sector contributes to about 59% of the total cloth production in 
the country.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need for early completion of Teesta Irrigation-cum-Energy Project in West 
Bengal 
SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Sir, my special 
mention is on the need for an early completion of the Teesta Irrigation-cum-
Energy Project in West Bengal. 
Sir, the Teesta Irrigation-cum-Energy Project in West Bengal is one of 
the largest projects of its kind, but it remains neglected for a long period. The 
Central Government had taken up this project in early 1970s. However, right 
from the beginning, the project has witnessed unnecessary delays and it took 
more than half a decade to start the project's work in 1977. Quarter of a 
century has passed since then, but more than 65 per cent of the project 
including the left bank canal still remains untouched and the cost has 
escalated over the years. The Project began with an initial estimated cost of 
nearly Rs. 70 crores. In the subsequent years, the West Bengal Government, 
within its limited resources, spent Rs. 833 crore while the Central 
Government's contribution remains Rs. 105 crore only. According to 
estimates, Rs. 700 crore is further needed to complete the project. 
The project would provide irrigation facilities to at least nine lakh 
hectares of land in six districts of Northern part of West Bengal. It would be a 
life-line for these areas where a majority of the population belongs to 
Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes and backward communities. 
I apprehend, if this slow pace of growth continues further, the very 
objective of this Teesta Project will be defeated. 
Hence, Sir, I request the Central Government to immediately take up 
the issue on priority basis to complete the project as soon as possible. This  
would  entail  immediate  release  of  sufficient  funds  by  the  Central 
Government.

Commission in its report is believed to have recommended reduction of 
holidays, which is welcome. The productivity in Government sector is 
historically low and holidays only aggravate the situation. Compared to other

prosperity depends on the work culture of its people. The Government will do

Problems of Poultry Farmers in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam. My Special Mention is about the problems of the poultry farmers in 
Andhra Pradesh. The State of Andhra Pradesh enjoys the topmost position in 
terms of poultry production "in the country, and is currently generating 
employment to millions of people in the rural areas. Mostly, the small and 
marginal farmers in the rural areas, are dependent on the poultry sector, as 
agriculture is a seasonal activity, and is to a large extent, dependent on 
monsoon. The Government of Andhra Pradesh has recognised the poultry 
industry as one of the major engines of growth in the development of the 
State, as per the "Vision 2020" document. Presently, the poultry farmers are 
facing critical problems of high input cost and low returns for their products, 
due to a steep rise in the price of maize. The Andhra Pradesh Poultry 
Federation made a representation on the need to protect the poultry industry, 
by taking the following steps:- 
By waiving of 15 per cent customs duty on the import of maize to 
meet the growing demands of the poultry sector; and by releasing 3 
lakh tonnes of wheat from the Food Corporation of India godowns at 
export rate, that is, Rs. 4350/- per metric ton, for the poultry farmers 
in Andhra Pradesh, instead of exporting the same.

a time when there are serious drought conditions prevailing in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh. This will also result in providing employment to lakhs of 
rural people. Unemployment is an area of major concern for the State, reeling 
under drought conditions. Thank you, Madam.

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam, for allowing me to speak on this very complex, complicated and 
crucial Bill, which seeks to protect our nation's biological interests. There are 
three basic goals of the Convention on Biodiversity. The first one is 
conservation. The second one is sustainable use of biological diversity. And, 
the third one is, fair and equitable sharing of the benefits, arising out of the 
utilisation of genetic resources. And, under Article 6 of this Convention, we 
are required to pass this legislation, which is before the House, since we are a 
signatory to the Convention. This Bill is one of a series of Bills -- the Patents 
(Second Amendment) Bill, the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' 
Rights Bill, the Geographic Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) 
Bill, etc. -- that this august House has approved. Unless you have a proper 
linkage and synergy between the above Bills and this Bill, we can achieve 
very little through this Bill. At the same time, the provisions of this Bill 
should also be harmonised with the licensing procedures for industries using 
biological resources, such as those falling under the provisions of the Drug 
and Cosmetics Act and other related Acts. 
Madam, as the House may be aware, India has one of the richest 
biodiversity in the world. It is recorded that out of 81,000 species of fauna and 
47,000 species of flora, 15,000 species are unique to India. The Indian Sub-
Continent contains about 25,000 species of vascular plants, of which, 7,500 
are used by foreign and other traditional systems of medicine. This clearly 
shows that our Sub-Continent, particularly India, occupies a unique position 
in the world and is capable of cultivating most of the medicinal plants used in 
the modern as well as traditional systems of medicine. The medicinal 
properties of some of the Indian herbs such as turmeric, neem, etc., are most

Madam, this legislation seeks to make necessary amendments to the

Sex determination techniques are used in India since 1975, primarily

were widely misused, to determine the sex of the foetus and subsequent 
abortions, if the foetus was female. In 1986, the Forum Against Sex 
Determination and Sex Pre-celection, a social action group, based in Mumbai, 
made a systematic attempt to initiate a campaign on this issue, pressuring the 
Maharashtra Government to enact the first-ever law in India. The Maharashtra 
Pre-Natal Diagnostic Technique Act was enacted in 1988. A Central 
legislation, based on this very Act, namely, the Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act. 1994, was brought in»o 
operation from 1* January 1996. Rules have also been framed under the Act. 
Under the existing Act, pre-natal diagnostic tests or procedures are allowed 
only for the purposes of detecting genetic or metabolic disorders or 
chromosomal abnormalities or congenital anomalies or sex-linked diseases,

adverse sex ratio of 927 females for 10 00 males, in the 0-6 age group, as 
revealed by the results of Census 2001. The pre-natal diagnostic techniques 
like amniocentesis and sonography are useful for the detection of genetic and

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I rise to support this Bill. We should hang our heads in shame 
that in the country of Bharat Mata, girls are killed even before their birth. 
From Vedas and other religious books, we find that women had a respectable 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
place in the society at that time. But now, female foeticide is increasing day 
by day. It has assumed an alarming proportion forcing the law-makers to 
discuss this problem in right earnest. Almost in every part of the country, the 
practice of female foeticide is taking place. In urban areas, female foeticide is 
done in subtle ways. In order to control this menace, we need to go deep into 
this problem. The major cause is dowry. As long as this practice is there in the 
society, this problem is not going to stop. To eradicate this social evil, we 
need to change our attitude. Law alone cannot help this. Religious leaders, 
Members of State Legislatures, social activists, and famous personalities 
should come forward to fight against this menace. In Punjab, the ratio of girls 
to boys has decreased from 882 : 1000 in 1991 to 874: 1000 in 2001. In 
Haryana also, the situation is dismal. But the silver lining in the dark clouds is 
that Akal Takht has issued a directive to the Sikh community to stop female 
foeticide. 
Another important aspect is encouragement. The Government should 
come forward and give suitable incentives to the families having girl children. 
In our State of Andhra Pradesh, the Government is already giving incentives 
to the parents having only female children. The State Government deposits 
some amount in the bank for the education of the girl child.   Besides, in 
Andhra Pradesh, women have equal property rights. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I take this opportunity to make certain 
suggestions. The medical community needs to take this legislation seriously. It 
should necessarily target these measures in order to effectively implement this 
legislation. The present Act does not define adequately the terms, 'genetic 
counselling centres', 'gene tic clinics' and 'genetic laboratories'. Though the 
proposed amendment to the Act defines the term 'medical genetics', it does not 
define the term 'genetic science'. I also request the hon. Minister that a course 
in genetics should be made compulsory in all medical colleges and 
institutions. As far as Advisory Board is concerned, the Central Supervisory 
Board should publish half-yearly reports about its functioning, and these 
reports should be made public to ensure accountability. Similarly, the 
appropriate authorities should submit their progress reports to the Central 
Supervisory Board. These progress reports should also be made public to 
ensure greater accountability. But women who are subjected to sex 
determination tests should not be punished, because, inadvertently, in most 
cases, they are the victims. I support this Bill wholeheartedly with an appeal to 
the Government to take concrete steps for giving suitable encouragement  and 
incentives to the girl child.    The

In the Statement of Objects and Reasons, in paragraph 3, it is

"It is, therefore, necessary to indicate and implement in

The main aim is to avoid the technique to be used before the

Objects and Reasons, it is mentioned:

sonography are useful..."

the pre-conception time.   The information

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Sir, I welcome this 
Bill. Since, it is a very serious matter, we should try to ensure 
implementation. Merely  passing  of  the  Bill  is  not  sufficient.    We  must  
ensure  proper implementation of the Bill.   The States should launch an 
effective awareness campaign to make the general public and service 
providers aware of the provisions of this Act.   The declining sex ratio is a 
matter of great concern. The declining sex ratio in the country is due to many 
socio-economic reasons and one important reason is non-preference in the 
family.   The family prefers to have a male child presuming that the female 
child would be a burden for the family.   The ultrasound is used all over the 
world. But, in Western countries, it is mainly used to check any deformity in 
the child, which may cause danger, so as to take precautions. 
But, in India, it is mainly used to identify the sex of the child to 
decide whether to pursue the pregnancy or not. It has been observed that the 
sex ratio has declined much more in the northern States as compared to the 
southern States. In the States of Haryana, Punjab and Delhi and in 
Chandigarh, the sex ratio is 820 women to 1000 men; 793 women to 1000 
men; 820 women to 1000 men and 793 men to 1000 men respectively. The 
sex ratio in India, which was 945 to 1000 in 1991, has declined to 927 to 1000 
in 2001. 
Madam, the present Bill is a very important one. Women have 
suffered a lot. There is a lot of violence against women, like domestic 
violence, molestation, rape, murder etc. The pre-natal diagnostic technique is 
also a kind of violence against them. Sometimes, they are forced to go in for 
MTP when they come to know that the sex of the child is female. 
All religious leaders have outrightly condemned the practice of 
female foeticide and said that it is an inhuman practice and should be stopped 
forthwith. 
The hon'ble Supreme Court has passed an order on 4 th May, 2001 
directing the registration of all bodies using the ultrasound equipments, under 
the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) 
Act, 1994. I do not know how far the States have complied with this direction.

this happens only after diagnosing and identifying that the child is a female

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala) : Madam. I have 
only two points. We all welcome the widening of the frontiers of friendship 
and co-operation with Russia. Of course, we consider that the interests of 
India can be better served in a multi-polar world. In this context, the Russian 
President has revived the proposal of a trilateral friendship arrangement 
between Russia, China and India. There were press reports to that effect. I 
would like to know whether the Russian President has made any concrete 
proposal with regard to this trilateral friendship between Russia, China and 
India and has he outlined the parameters of this trilateral friendship? 
The second query is related to a paragraph of the 'Delhi Declaration'. 
It is in the middle of page 4. I quote "we call tor early start of multilateral talks 
aimed at preparing a comprehensive arrangement on non-deployment of 
weapons in outer space, non-use or threat of use of force in respect of space-
based objecis and preserving the use of space for full

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam, I whole-
heartedly welcome the statement and the initiatives taken by the Prime 
Minister during the visit of the President of the Russian Federation. The joint 
statement and the Delhi Declaration clearly outline the long-standing 
relationship between these two great countries. In fact, I do not want to seek 
any clarification. I would just like to place on record our appreciation on the 
visit of President Putin and the way he endorsed our stand in regard to 
combating international cross-border terrorism. The type of support which we 
expected from the international community, which we were getting in the 
earlier days, has been doubly reinforced during the visit of President Putin. It 
was needed much more. I am glad that the Prime Minister had highlighted the 
agreement which we signed in the early 90s for the repayment of debts.

spite of all this, we wanted to sell our tea, tobacco,

Madam, I come to the point that the nomenclature of the Bill has 
been changed, from "Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and 
Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994" to "Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act". The reason behind 
this change, as the hon. Member, Shri Shunmugasundaram also mentioned, is 
that the technology available in the country has forced us to change the 
nomenclature so that the general public, the para-medical and medical 
personnel, comprehend the purpose and the message of the Act from reading 
the title of the Act itself. Earlier, what was being done in the medical field -- 
as Shrimati S.G. Indira also mentioned - was, whether it was an embryo or a 
substance in the womb, we could identify whether it was a male or a female 
foetus. Now, a technology has come whereby, even without going into the 
womb or the fallopian tube or the embryo, one can ensure the conception of a 
male child. It can be done by disconnecting the 'X' and 'Y' chromosomes. 
What is done is, the *X' and Y chromosomes of a man are separated, and the 
T  c h r o m o s o m e  i s  f u s e d  w i t h  a  w oman's chromosome, to ensure the 
conception of a male child. So, because this advanced technology has come, 
the law is also required to be changed accordingly. It is with this end in view 
that the nomenclature has been changed and, also, appropriate sections have 
been incorporated in the Act. 
Then, apprehensions were expressed whether this law will also 
punish people in the case of diagnostic tests carried out for reasons other than 
female foeticide. On that, Madam, the law is very clear. So far as regulation, 
as contemplated in the Act, is concerned, we have no difficulty with regard to 
genetic and metabolic disorders; we have no difficulty in regard to 
chromosomal abnormalities or congenital malformations or sex-linked 
disorders. Certainly, the use of ultrasound machines for pre-natal diagnosis is

the Act itself. When discussions were held in the  Ministry, all these aspects 
were considered; there are diagnostic tests in respect of 23 contexts like 
diagnosis of intra-urine and acoptic (?) pregnancy and so on that have been 
exempted in the Act.

expressed doubts whether any provision is available in the PNDT Act. to deal 
with illegal and unsafe abortions. My submission is that these apprehensions 
and doubts have been addressed in the MTP Act, where penal provisions are 
available.

conclusion. The conclusion drawn by the Divisional Commissioner and that 
of the National Commission for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
are almost similar, identical. Both the Inquiry Reports say that it was certainly 
not an incident of atrocities against Dalits, but, on the other hand, it was 
because of the misinterpretation, mi sconception, misinformation, rumour-
mongering in that area. Why did the crowd gather from so many villages and 
all that? It was also a coincidence because of the Dussehra festival. One of the 
hon. Members has put it pointedly as to how so many people have collected at 
one place. On the Dussehra festival - and Jhajjhar being the district 
headquarters; in each village, Dussehra festival is not celebrated, Dussehra 
mela is not held; it is held at sub-divisional or district headquarters - it so 
happened that from many villages, the people gathered there and they were 
coming back. That was the situation there. 
So far as the negligence or the connivance etc., of the police officials 
and the Executive in the State and other officers is concerned, including the 
DSP, of course, the Divisional Commissioner has also come to the same 
conclusion and the National Commission on Scheduled Castes has also 
mentioned that there was an under-estimation and they could not estimate that 
the crowd would swell so much; they had a small post, comprising of an ASI 
and 4 to 10 constables. They never expected this; but when the force came, at 
that time also, they under-estimated and that has been pointed out by both the 
reports. That is why, on the basis of the reports, all the officers are being 
chargesheeted for major penalties, not for minor penalties. Whatever other 
actions are suggested now by the hon. Members, they are for the State 
Government to consider. You will appreciate this. 
Another query which has been made is, why not an inquiry be done by 
the CBI? I am sure you will appreciate the position of law. All the hon. 
Members,  who have pointed it out, would be knowing that under the 
270 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
provisions of the law, the Central Government has no power to initiate an 
action or direct in any particular case that that should be given to the CBI. It is 
for the State Governments. If they want an inquiry in a particular case, where 
the matter, the situation, the facts are very complicated, where they feel that 
they must pass on the case for an inquiry by the CBI, then only the cases are 
sent to the CBI. Without the consent of the State Government, the Central 
Government can't transfer any case for investigation to the CBI. Of course, 
we have, luckily, in this country, not only a democratic polity but also we 
have an independent and very learned judiciary. Judicial forums are always 
available for anybody who feels aggrieved. But so far as these five families 
are concerned, I can assure you that they are satisfied. 
Of course, it was a very heinous incident, it was a very unfortunate 
incident, but it happened not because of any organisation, not because of any 
other reason. Mr. Malik has rightly pointed out. I also have checked it up 
from the record. I know that when the case was registered against 23 persons, 
four of them belonged to the Scheduled Castes. People from other castes were 
also there, because some of the villages surrounding that area are dominated, 
by the Jat community and other communities as well. Yes, many people are 
there from this community. 
When cases were registered against these people, when these people 
were brought, they were arrested. Then it came to light that four or five of 
them certainly belonged to the Scheduled Castes. They, are also accused in 
this. At the time thtf'incident happened, it was not a question of atrocity 
against dalits. Nobody would presume that dalits would start beating or 
burning or killing a<person of their own caste; not at all. It was only because 
the people mistook it as slaughter of a cow. On the slaughter of a, cow, you 
know the sentiments of the people, especially in the rural areas; sentiments 
run very high. If the cows are being slaughtered in an open place, publicly, 
nobody is going to tolerate it, Whatever be the area, especially in the rural 
areas. The sentiments ran.very high. That is the point. As mentioned in my 
statement, the inquiry report of the Commissioner, the Divisional 
Commissioner, says the same thing-it was because of this and not because of 
atrocities against dalits at all. 
About Haryana, I again repeat what I have said in my statement. 
Really, the situation is such that there are no serious offences, no complaints 
at all, no such feelings amongst the communities on the basis of caste or creed 
or even religion. We have the area of Mewat, where a lot of Muslim  brothers 
live;  there are villages dominated by Muslim brothers; 
271 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December. 2002] 
Hindus also are living there. Even in that area, there is no such animosity, 
there is no such complaint at all. That is why I said, in Haryana we have been 
traditionally living in peace. The unfortunate incident which happened on that 
day was because of an impression that cows were being slaughtered in the 
open place. That is why all this happened. 
So far as the other allegations are concerned, Ghoriwala or the story of 
riot, etc., which was also pointed out, I can certainly say that they are only 
baseless stories. They did appear in the newspapers; I have also read them. I 
tried to verify from the families, and from the people who had come to Karnal 
to pay their condolence or for the mourning, etc. I inquired from them also 
and nobody could verify it. I don't know wherefrom they landed. There was 
no such thing. Yes, negligence has been there; callousness has been there on 
the part of the police officers. Yes, their under-estimation of the situation was 
there. Nobody would deny it. That is why the State Government has agreed in 
toto with the  Report of the Judicial Commissioner and all the officers are 
being chargesheeted. That is all I can say at this time.    And I

SHRI I.D. SWAMI: One thing, which was also pointed out, that how 
those two bodies were burnt and whether post-mortem was done. A post-
mortem was conducted on all the five bodies by a board of doctors and all the 
injuries are ante-mortem, except in one case where one person was thrown on 
fire and the death was because of burn injuries. In the other cases, there were 
no burn injuries. To clinch the issue, even the postmortem was carried out on 
the dead animal, the dead cow so that there was no question of slaughter and 
all that and it showed that for more than 24 hours the cow was dead. It was a 
dead cow which was skinned. Unfortunately, a rumour lead to this unfortunate 
incident which has, to be condemned, which has been condemned by the 
whole House. But I can  assure this august House that in Haryana except this 
incident, --in the recent past also -- there is no animosity in that State. I also 
belong to Haryana, and at least, I know the situation there. There is no 
animosity at all in that State.   The people are living in peace and I hope and 
pray that 
272 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
they would continue to live in peace not only in Haryana, but also in the 
whole country. So far as this incident is concerned, we must condemn it. The 
officers who have been negligent or callous or indifferent or who did not 
estimate the situation properly, they are being punished. That also is very 
sure. But so far the use of water cannons is concerned, the use of teargas is 
concerned, unfortunately, in small stations the police force is minimal, 
nowhere, I think, these things are available. They cannot be brought 
immediately from the District Headquarters or from other far away place, 
where our police lines are or where the Haryana Armed Police stays, that is, at 
Madhuban in Kamal. That could not have been done. And they did not 
estimate it. Perhaps, that action could have been taken by the DM or the SP. 
But this was not the estimation and that is why this has happened, this 
unfortunate incident has happened. And there is no doubt about it. We ail 
should condemn it. So far as the officers are concerned, they will be punished 
and nobody will be spared.   Thank you.
